title: Installing the CloudNativePG Operator
description: This lab builds you a fresh 3-node k3d cluster with no operator installed and the CloudNativePG release manifest staged on the server node. Install CloudNativePG by applying it, wait for its CRDs and webhook to come up, and confirm exactly which build is running before trusting it.
lectureNotes:
What CloudNativePG is

CloudNativePG (CNPG) is a Kubernetes operator for PostgreSQL: instead of a human running pg_basebackup, editing recovery.conf, and wiring up a load balancer by hand, you describe the PostgreSQL cluster you want as a single Cluster custom resource, and the operator continuously reconciles real Kubernetes objects (Pods, PVCs, Services, Secrets) to match it. It is a control loop, the same pattern every Kubernetes controller uses — watch, compare desired vs. actual, act, repeat.

How it actually gets installed: one manifest, applied server-side

Upstream CNPG can be installed from a Helm chart or from the release manifest that ships inside each tagged release — and the manifest is the method CNPG's own Quickstart and e2e test suite use, so it is the one this lab teaches. The release source is already staged on the server node, which makes the entire install a single command: `kubectl apply --server-side -f /root/cloudnative-pg/releases/cnpg-1.30.0.yaml`. That one file creates the `cnpg-system` namespace, every `postgresql.cnpg.io` CRD (11 of them — clusters, backups, scheduledbackups, poolers, and more), the RBAC the operator needs, and a single-replica operator Deployment named `cnpg-controller-manager`.

The `--server-side` flag is not decoration. A client-side apply stores the whole manifest it sent back on the object, in a `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation — and CNPG's CRDs are far too big to fit inside Kubernetes' 256 KB annotation limit, so the apply fails outright. Server-side apply tracks field ownership on the API server instead, which is why large-CRD operator installs need it.

The CRDs vs. the webhook

CRDs registering is not the same as the operator being ready to use. CNPG validates and defaults every Cluster you create through an admission webhook served by the operator Pod itself — so a Cluster applied in the gap between "CRDs exist" and "operator Pod is actually Running" fails outright with `no endpoints available for service "cnpg-webhook-service"`. In practice the CRDs establish almost instantly (all 11 share one timestamp), while the operator Pod still needs several seconds to schedule, start and pass its readiness probe — so the real ordering constraint is "wait for the Pod", not "wait for the CRDs". (This environment side-loads the operator image into every node before the lab starts, so that wait is process startup, not a registry download.)

Why verify the running version explicitly

The manifest is named for a version (`cnpg-1.30.0.yaml`), but what actually reconciles your `Cluster` resources is whichever image the Deployment ended up running — and a manifest fetched from a moving reference, re-applied over an older install, or partially applied does not guarantee the two agree. Reading the running image back with `kubectl -n cnpg-system get deploy cnpg-controller-manager -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'` is the same check a promotion pipeline runs before trusting a freshly-provisioned cluster — trust what's actually running, not what you asked for.

steps.title: Install and verify the operator
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Survey the cluster with `kubectl get nodes -o wide`, then install the operator from the release manifest already staged on the server node:

```
kubectl apply --server-side -f /root/cloudnative-pg/releases/cnpg-1.30.0.yaml
```

Wait for `kubectl -n cnpg-system get pods` to show 1/1 Running, confirm the CRDs with `kubectl get crd | grep cnpg.io`, and confirm the exact image with `kubectl -n cnpg-system get deploy cnpg-controller-manager -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'`, then click Check Work.
steps.hint: If the operator Pod is still ContainerCreating, give it a few more seconds — and if the apply itself failed, check that you passed `--server-side`; CNPG's CRDs are too large for a client-side apply.

title: Creating a Cluster
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with the CloudNativePG operator already installed and a Cluster manifest staged but not applied. Apply it, watch the operator bootstrap 3 instances into a healthy state, and prove with real SQL that writes replicate.
lectureNotes:
The whole spec is five lines

A CNPG Cluster manifest asking for 3 instances and 1Gi of storage per instance is genuinely just:

```yaml
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: pg-cluster
spec:
  instances: 3
  storage:
    size: 1Gi
```

Everything else — the StatefulSet-like Pod management, one PVC per instance, the `-rw`/`-ro`/`-r` Services, the `<name>-app` credentials Secret, streaming replication between instances — the operator generates and wires up on its own.

What the phase string is actually telling you

`kubectl get cluster` reports a human-readable STATUS that moves through real, named phases: "Setting up primary" (instance 1 running initdb), "Creating a new replica" (instance 2 joining via streaming replication), "Waiting for the instances to become active" (instance 3 joining), and finally "Cluster in healthy state" once all 3 report ready. This whole sequence takes several minutes, and not because Postgres itself is slow to start: CNPG bootstraps one instance at a time — `initdb` on the primary, then a join job per replica — so the work is serial by design. Image caching normally compounds it, since each of the 3 k3s nodes keeps an entirely separate container image cache and would otherwise pull the Postgres image once per node; this environment side-loads it into all three up front, so that cost is paid before the lab starts rather than during it.

Who the primary actually is, and why it matters

Exactly one instance is designated primary (labeled `cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary`) and accepts writes; the rest stream from it as replicas and serve reads. The operator's own anti-affinity rules spread all 3 instances across distinct nodes automatically for a cluster this size — no `topologySpreadConstraint` required. A healthy `Cluster` object is a necessary condition for a working database, not a sufficient one: the only real proof is writing through SQL on the primary and reading the same row back from a replica.

steps.title: Apply, wait, and verify
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes (the operator is already installed).

Review and apply the manifest already on the node:

```
cat cluster.yaml
kubectl apply -f cluster.yaml
```

Poll `kubectl get cluster` until STATUS reads "Cluster in healthy state" and READY is 3/3, then `kubectl get pods -L cnpg.io/instanceRole` to find the primary. Prove it end to end: `kubectl exec <primary> -c postgres -- psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U app -d app -c "CREATE TABLE pv_proof (id serial primary key, note text, created_at timestamptz default now());"`, insert a row with `RETURNING *`, then read it back from a different instance, and click Check Work.
steps.hint: `kubectl get pods -L cnpg.io/instanceRole` — the column reads `primary` for exactly one pod; writing to any other pod fails with "cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction".

title: Usage of a Persistent Volume for Data Storage
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy 3-instance CloudNativePG cluster. Inspect the PVC backing the primary, write data, delete the primary Pod outright, and prove the same PVC — not a fresh one — survives the failover with the data intact.
lectureNotes:
One PVC per instance, provisioned automatically

CNPG creates exactly one PersistentVolumeClaim per instance Pod, named identically to the Pod (`pg-cluster-1`, `pg-cluster-2`, `pg-cluster-3`). On a plain k3s cluster these bind against the bundled `local-path` StorageClass — nothing CNPG-specific, the same provisioner every vanilla k3s install ships with.

`local-path` is node-local storage, not a portable cloud volume

This is the detail worth internalizing: `local-path` provisions a `hostPath` directory on whichever node the Pod is first scheduled to (`WaitForFirstConsumer` binding), recorded on the PVC as a `volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node` annotation. It behaves nothing like a real cloud CSI driver's volumes, which can reattach to any node in the cluster. If the pinned node ever left the cluster, that PVC could never rebind — a constraint worth teaching explicitly rather than letting learners assume PVCs are always freely portable.

Why deleting the Pod, not the data, still proves persistence

Deleting a CNPG instance Pod outright (not cordoning, not draining) is a faithful stand-in for a crash or an OOM-kill. CNPG promotes a healthy replica to primary almost immediately, and the deleted Pod's replacement is recreated — and because `local-path` only binds to its pinned node, Kubernetes reschedules the replacement Pod back onto that exact same node, where its exact same PVC and underlying PV are still sitting untouched. That's the real proof: not that the PVC *exists* afterward, but that it is the *same* PVC (same volume name, same age) as before, holding the same data. A fresh volume with the same name would be a very different (and much worse) outcome.

steps.title: Break it on purpose and prove the data survives
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes (a healthy 3-instance Cluster is already running).

Inspect the PVCs with `kubectl get pvc` and `kubectl describe pvc <primary-pod>` — note the `volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node` annotation. Write a row into a new table on the primary, confirm it replicated to a replica, then delete the primary Pod outright: `kubectl delete pod <primary-pod>`.

Watch `kubectl get cluster` and `kubectl get pods -o wide` until healthy again, confirm via `kubectl get pvc` that the recreated Pod's PVC is the exact same volume (not a new one), read the original row back from the recreated Pod, and finally insert a new row through the `-rw` Service (which now points at the newly-promoted primary) and confirm every instance sees both rows. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The recreated Pod comes back as a replica, never as the primary again — a different instance gets promoted the moment the original primary disappears.

title: Connecting via Services, Including Read-Only
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy 3-instance CloudNativePG cluster and a separate client Pod. Read what each of the three generated Services actually resolves to, write through the read-write one, watch the read-only one refuse the same statement, and count the endpoints behind each.
lectureNotes:
Three Services, one database

For every Cluster it manages, CloudNativePG creates three Services, and picking the wrong one is one of the easiest ways to build an application that works in testing and fails in production. `<cluster>-rw` resolves to the primary and is the only one that accepts writes. `<cluster>-ro` resolves to the replicas, and only the replicas. `<cluster>-r` resolves to every instance, primary included.

They are not special objects. Each is an ordinary ClusterIP Service whose entire behaviour comes from its selector: `-rw` selects `cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary`, `-ro` selects `cnpg.io/instanceRole=replica`, and `-r` selects `cnpg.io/podRole=instance`, which every instance Pod carries. The operator maintains those labels; Kubernetes recomputes the endpoint sets continuously from them. That is the whole mechanism, and it is why the write endpoint follows a failover without anything reconnecting to a new address by name.

What a wrong choice looks like at run time

Sending a write to `-ro` does not produce a routing error, because nothing is misrouted: the connection reaches a real PostgreSQL instance, which happens to be a streaming replica permanently in recovery. PostgreSQL itself refuses the statement, with `ERROR: cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction`. The failure therefore shows up at the first write, at run time, in an application whose reads have been working perfectly — which is precisely why it is worth provoking once, deliberately, before meeting it by accident.

When to use -ro rather than -r

Both serve reads, and the difference is whether the primary is in the set. `-ro` has as many endpoints as there are replicas and never includes the primary, so it is the right target for reporting queries, dashboards and anything else whose load you want kept away from the instance taking writes. `-r` includes the primary, so it spreads reads across every instance — useful when any instance will do and you would rather use all of the capacity. Neither offers read-your-own-write guarantees: replication here is asynchronous, so a read routed to a replica may not yet see a row committed a moment ago on the primary.

steps.title: Read, write, and be refused
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

List the Services with `kubectl get svc -o wide` and read their selectors, then look up the endpoints behind each with `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=pg-cluster-rw`. From the `psql-client` Pod, create a table and write a row through `pg-cluster-rw`, read it back through `pg-cluster-ro`, then send the same INSERT to `pg-cluster-ro` and capture the error. Count the endpoints behind `pg-cluster-ro` and `pg-cluster-r`, and click Check Work.
steps.hint: `pg-cluster-ro` has one endpoint per replica and never includes the primary; `pg-cluster-r` includes every instance.

title: Connecting with Client Certificates
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy CloudNativePG cluster with its own certificate authority, the cnpg plugin installed, and a client Pod manifest staged but not applied. Issue a client certificate for the app user, turn on certificate authentication declaratively, and connect with no password at all.
lectureNotes:
Every cluster is its own certificate authority

A CloudNativePG cluster generates a private CA the moment it is created, and issues itself everything it needs from it. `<cluster>-ca` holds `ca.crt` and `ca.key`. `<cluster>-server` holds the certificate PostgreSQL presents to clients, issued for the read-write Service name with subject alternative names covering all three Service names in short and fully-qualified form. `<cluster>-replication` holds a client certificate that the replicas use to authenticate as the `streaming_replica` user — so certificate authentication is already in use inside the cluster before you touch anything.

That the server certificate is issued for a Service name rather than a Pod name is the detail that makes verification workable: a client using `sslmode=verify-full` checks the name it dialled against the certificate, and the name it dialled is a Service that survives any instance being replaced.

A certificate is not permission

Issuing a client certificate changes nothing on its own. PostgreSQL decides how each connection may authenticate from `pg_hba.conf`, and the default rules the operator writes accept certificates only from `streaming_replica` and the pooler role; everything else falls through to a password rule at the end of the file. Adding `hostssl app app all cert` is what makes a client certificate mean something for an application user.

You never edit that file. The operator owns it and would reconcile a hand edit away, so the rule goes in the Cluster resource under `spec.postgresql.pg_hba`, and the operator writes it out and reloads every instance — no restart, no downtime. Two consequences follow. `pg_hba` is first match wins, and the operator always appends its password-based catch-all last, so a rule placed there is reachable. And once the rule is in place, a TLS connection carrying a correct password but no client certificate is refused outright, with `FATAL: connection requires a valid client certificate` — the password has not become wrong, it has become insufficient.

Proving which credential was used

Asserting that a connection authenticated by certificate is easy to get wrong, because a connection that would have succeeded with a password looks identical from the outside. PostgreSQL exposes `pg_stat_ssl`, which reports for the current session whether TLS is in use, which protocol version, and the distinguished name read from the client certificate — `/CN=app`. Writing that value into a table from inside the session is the strongest available proof: it is the server's own account of who connected, not the client's.

steps.title: Issue, enable, connect
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Inspect the operator-generated Secrets, then read the certificate the database presents on the wire with `kubectl exec pg-cluster-1 -c postgres -- sh -c "openssl s_client -starttls postgres -connect pg-cluster-rw:5432 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer"`. Issue a client certificate with `kubectl cnpg certificate app-client-cert --cnpg-cluster pg-cluster --cnpg-user app`, add a `hostssl app app all cert` rule to `spec.postgresql.pg_hba`, confirm a password-only TLS connection is now refused, then apply `/root/cert-client.yaml` and connect with `sslmode=verify-full` and the certificate. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The plugin flags are `--cnpg-cluster` and `--cnpg-user`; `--cluster` and `--user` belong to kubectl itself.

title: Serving Your Own Server Certificate
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy CloudNativePG cluster that serves TLS with a certificate it generated for itself. Become the certificate authority instead: create a CA with openssl, issue a server certificate for the cluster's Service names, hand both to the operator, and prove on the wire that the old CA no longer validates anything.
lectureNotes:
Why replace a certificate that already works

A CloudNativePG cluster is its own certificate authority from the moment it is created: it generates a self-signed CA, issues itself a server certificate from it, and serves TLS immediately. That is excellent for getting started and useless for verification, because the CA exists only inside the cluster. A client outside it has no reason to trust that CA, so in practice it either skips verification entirely — leaving the connection encrypted but unauthenticated, and open to being intercepted — or has the generated CA copied around by hand every time the cluster is rebuilt. Supplying your own certificate, from a CA your clients already trust, is what makes `sslmode=verify-full` a realistic setting rather than an aspiration.

What the certificate has to say

Two fields decide whether a hand-issued certificate works. The common name must be the cluster's read-write Service name, because that is the name the operator's own tooling and the instances themselves expect. The subject alternative names must cover every Service name a client might dial — the read-write, read-only and read Services, in short, namespaced and fully-qualified form. A client using full verification checks the host name it dialled against those names, so a certificate that names only one Service silently breaks every client connecting through another. Getting this wrong is the single most common failure in a hand-rolled setup, and it fails at connection time rather than at apply time.

OpenSSL 3 makes the issuing part short: one command generates a key and a self-signed CA, and a second generates the server key and signs it with that CA in the same step, with `-addext` carrying the alternative names.

How it is handed over

The operator reads two Secrets, named in `spec.certificates`. `serverCASecret` is an ordinary Secret with the CA certificate under the key `ca.crt`. `serverTLSSecret` is a `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret holding the certificate and its key — the same shape the operator generates for itself. The CA's private key never has to leave the machine that signs with it; the operator has no use for it.

Both are named together for a reason worth understanding. The replicas verify the primary's certificate against the server CA the operator gives them, so this is not only a client-facing setting: handing over a certificate without the CA that signed it would break streaming replication, not just external clients.

What the change costs

Nothing, in the sense that matters: the operator replaces the mounted material and has PostgreSQL reload its configuration. No instance restarts, no Pod is recreated, restart counts stay at zero and replication keeps streaming. Verifying the result is worth doing on the wire rather than from the Secret — open a TLS handshake against the read-write Service and read the certificate the server actually presents. Connecting afterwards with `verify-full` against the new CA succeeds; connecting against the operator's original CA fails with `SSL error: certificate verify failed`, which is the honest demonstration that the trust anchor has moved.

steps.title: Issue and install your own server certificate
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Inside the `psql-client` Pod (the nodes carry no openssl), create a self-signed CA and issue a server certificate from it with `CN=pg-cluster-rw` and subject alternative names covering all three Services. Copy the PEMs out with `kubectl exec psql-client -- cat <file> > <local>`, create `pg-server-ca` (`--from-file=ca.crt=...`) and `pg-server-cert` (`kubectl create secret tls`), then name both in `spec.certificates`. Confirm the cluster stays healthy and replication keeps streaming, read the presented certificate with `openssl s_client -starttls postgres`, and check that `verify-full` succeeds against your CA and fails against the operator's. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The alternative names decide whether clients can verify at all — cover pg-cluster-rw, pg-cluster-ro and pg-cluster-r.

title: Connection Pooling with PgBouncer
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy CloudNativePG cluster, a client Pod, and a Pooler manifest staged but not applied. Apply it, watch the operator build PgBouncer from it, route real traffic through the pooled Service, and measure how many PostgreSQL backends your connections actually share.
lectureNotes:
Why a pooler at all

PostgreSQL serves every connection with its own operating-system process, forked from the postmaster and given its own memory. That model is robust and it is expensive: a few thousand short-lived connections, of the kind a horizontally scaled application produces, spend most of their cost on setting up and tearing down backends. A connection pooler keeps a small number of server connections open and lends them to clients, so the expensive part happens once.

The Pooler resource

In CloudNativePG you do not deploy PgBouncer; you declare a `Pooler` and the operator builds it. The resource names the cluster to sit in front of, how many PgBouncer instances to run, whether it follows the primary (`type: rw`) or the replicas (`type: ro`), and the PgBouncer settings themselves. From that the operator creates a Deployment, its Pods, and a Service named after the Pooler — which is the name applications connect to from then on.

Running more than one instance matters more than it might seem: a pooler sits on the path of every connection, so a single replica would reintroduce a single point of failure in front of a highly available database.

Authentication is wired up for you

The usual friction of running PgBouncer is credentials — a `userlist.txt` to maintain, or an auth query and a role to own it. The operator does this itself: when a Pooler exists it creates a dedicated `cnpg_pooler_pgbouncer` role in the database and gives PgBouncer a client certificate to authenticate with, which is why the cluster's own default `pg_hba` rules already include a `hostssl` certificate rule for that role. Clients keep using their ordinary credentials.

Pool modes, and what reuse actually looks like

`session` pooling returns a server connection to the pool only when the client disconnects; `transaction` pooling returns it at the end of every transaction, which multiplies reuse but breaks anything relying on session state — prepared statements, session-level advisory locks, temporary tables, LISTEN and NOTIFY. The effect is measurable in one query: ask `pg_backend_pid()` over several separate connections. Straight to the database, six connections give six distinct backends. Through a two-instance pooler, the same six give at most two — one per PgBouncer Pod, since each keeps its own pool and the Service spreads clients across both. PgBouncer's own admin console, reachable over a unix socket inside each Pod, reports the same thing from its side: client connections held, server connections in use, and where each pool points — which for a `type: rw` pooler is the cluster's read-write Service, so it follows a failover without knowing anything about one.

steps.title: Apply a Pooler and measure the reuse
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Read and apply `/root/pooler.yaml`, then watch `kubectl get pooler`, `kubectl get deploy pg-cluster-pooler-rw` and its Pods come up. From the `psql-client` Pod, write a row through `pg-cluster-pooler-rw` and confirm `inet_server_addr()` is the primary. Query PgBouncer's admin console with `kubectl exec <pooler-pod> -c pgbouncer -- psql -h /controller/run -U pgbouncer pgbouncer -c "SHOW POOLS;"`, then compare `pg_backend_pid()` over six connections through the pooler against six straight to `pg-cluster-rw`. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The admin console listens on a unix socket, not the network: `-h /controller/run -U pgbouncer pgbouncer`.

title: Failover
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy 3-instance CloudNativePG cluster and a client Pod. Map the replication topology, write a row that matters, then destroy the primary outright and watch an unplanned promotion happen on a new timeline — with the other replica re-attaching and the destroyed instance rejoining as a replica.
lectureNotes:
What the operator is actually watching

CloudNativePG runs a control loop over the Cluster resource: it compares the instances that should exist and the roles they should hold against what is really there, and acts on the difference. When the primary Pod disappears, nothing needs to be told — the difference is visible, a healthy replica is chosen, and it is promoted. The `cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary` label moves with it, which is what moves the read-write Service's endpoint, because that Service is nothing but a selector over that label.

Deleting a Pod with `--grace-period=0 --force` is a fair stand-in for the failure this is meant to survive: an out-of-memory kill, a hypervisor losing a node, a kernel panic. It is not a cordon or a drain, and no part of it asks for a failover.

Timelines: how PostgreSQL records a promotion

When a standby is promoted it starts a new timeline, incrementing the timeline ID and writing a history file. This is not bookkeeping — it is what makes it impossible for two instances to diverge silently along the same line of history. A cluster that has never had a promotion is on timeline 1; after one failover it is on timeline 2. Because a Pod restart alone never changes it, the timeline is the single most honest number for answering "did a promotion really happen here?"

The other replica, and the one that comes back

A failover is not only about the promoted instance. The replica that was not chosen has to re-attach to a primary it was never told about, and follow the new timeline; CloudNativePG reconfigures it to do so. The instance that was destroyed is recreated by the operator, discovers the cluster has moved on, and rejoins as a replica — it does not take its old role back, and it does not need to be re-cloned from a base backup as long as it can follow the new timeline from where the two diverged. `pg_stat_replication` on the new primary is where you confirm all of this: two rows, both streaming, one of them the instance you destroyed.

What asynchronous replication means for the row you wrote

This cluster replicates asynchronously, so a commit returns as soon as the primary has flushed it locally — it does not wait for any replica. A row is present on both replicas because they are caught up, not because the commit required it. That is the honest framing for the data-survival check: on an idle cluster the replicas are current and nothing is lost, while a write-heavy cluster losing its primary mid-commit is exactly the case synchronous replication exists to address.

steps.title: Destroy the primary and watch the promotion
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Find the primary with `kubectl get pods -L cnpg.io/instanceRole` and ask it `SELECT application_name, state, sync_state FROM pg_stat_replication;` as the postgres superuser. Write a row noted 'before-failover' through `pg-cluster-rw` and confirm both replicas have it. Then `kubectl delete pod <primary> --grace-period=0 --force`, watch the promotion and the endpoint move, wait for the cluster to report healthy again, and confirm the timeline advanced from 1 to 2 with the row intact. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The instance you destroy comes back as a replica — the promoted one keeps the role.

title: Switchover
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy 3-instance CloudNativePG cluster with the cnpg plugin installed. Check the replicas are caught up, choose which one takes over, hand the role across deliberately, and confirm the old primary came back as a replica on its own original volume rather than being rebuilt.
lectureNotes:
The planned move, and why the order of operations matters

A switchover is the handover you perform before draining a node, patching a kernel, or retiring a machine. Unlike a failover it is initiated, and it happens in a deliberate order: the current primary is shut down cleanly first, so it stops accepting writes and flushes everything it holds, and only then is the chosen replica promoted, having replayed the last of that WAL. That ordering is why a planned switchover loses nothing, where an unplanned failover can only promise as much as replication had already delivered.

It is still a promotion. The timeline advances exactly as it would after a crash, from 1 to 2, and the read-write Service's endpoint follows the `cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary` label onto the new instance within a couple of seconds.

How you ask for one

The cnpg kubectl plugin's `promote` command takes the cluster and the instance that should take over. What it does underneath is small enough to be worth knowing: it sets the cluster's target primary to the instance you named, and the operator's control loop reconciles reality to match — which is why the command returns immediately while the work happens asynchronously, and why the cluster reports "Switchover in progress" while it does.

Demoted, not rebuilt

The most consequential detail is what happens to the instance that used to be primary. It restarts once and rejoins as a replica of the instance you promoted, and it keeps its own PersistentVolumeClaim — same volume, same data, same age. It catches up by replaying WAL from the point where the two histories diverged, not by taking a fresh base backup.

That distinction decides whether a switchover costs seconds or costs as long as cloning the whole database, and it is worth verifying rather than assuming: check that the claim behind the demoted instance is the one it always had, and that it now appears in `pg_stat_replication` on the new primary. An instance that had been re-cloned would look healthy too — it would just have cost you a full copy of the database to get there.

Checking it is safe first

Before handing over, confirm there is a replica worth handing to: both replicas streaming, LSNs matching the primary's, and the lag columns at zero. The plugin's `status` command shows exactly that in one screen, and `pg_stat_replication` on the primary is the same information from PostgreSQL directly.

steps.title: Hand the primary role across
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Check the replicas are caught up with `kubectl cnpg status pg-cluster` and `SELECT application_name, state, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;` on the primary. Write a row noted 'before-switchover' through `pg-cluster-rw`, then hand the role across with `kubectl cnpg promote pg-cluster pg-cluster-2`. Watch the status move through "Switchover in progress" and back to healthy, confirm the old primary is now a replica reusing its original PVC, then write again through `pg-cluster-rw` and confirm all 3 instances see both rows. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The argument order is the cluster first, then the instance: `kubectl cnpg promote pg-cluster <instance>`.

title: Primary Endpoint Switch in Under 10 Seconds
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy 3-instance CloudNativePG cluster and a client Pod. Record where the write endpoint points, destroy the primary while timing how long the endpoint takes to name a different Pod, and check your stopwatch against the operator's own promotion timestamps.
lectureNotes:
The claim being tested

CloudNativePG's own end-to-end suite asserts that after an unplanned failover the write endpoint follows the new primary in under ten seconds. This lab reproduces that measurement on a real cluster rather than quoting it, which is worth doing because it is the number an application actually experiences: not how long a promotion takes internally, but how long a client holding the read-write Service name is unable to write.

What happens in those seconds

Four things, in order. The operator notices the primary is gone. It chooses a replica and promotes it, which starts a new timeline. It moves the `cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary` label onto the promoted instance. Kubernetes recomputes the Service's endpoints from that label. Only the last of those touches the Service, and it is the cheapest — most of the elapsed time is detection.

A detail worth expecting: between the primary disappearing and the promotion completing, the write endpoint is briefly empty rather than stale. An empty endpoint set is how Kubernetes stops traffic reaching a database that currently has no primary, and it is the correct behaviour — connections are refused instead of being routed somewhere that would refuse the write anyway.

Measuring it honestly

The timing has to start at the deletion, in the same shell, without a human in the loop — starting a stopwatch by hand in another terminal measures reflexes rather than the cluster. Deleting with `--wait=false` matters for the same reason: the default blocks until the Pod is gone, so the clock would start after the interesting part had begun. A one-second poll of the endpoint is precise enough for a ten-second budget and needs nothing but kubectl.

The cluster's own stopwatch

There is a second measurement that does not depend on anyone timing anything. The Cluster status carries `targetPrimaryTimestamp`, stamped when the operator decided there should be a new primary, and `currentPrimaryTimestamp`, stamped when that instance actually became one. The gap between them is the promotion itself — typically under a second on an idle cluster — and the difference between that and what you measured is detection plus the endpoint update. Those two stamps are also how this lab is graded, so the claim is checked against the cluster's own record rather than against a number a learner typed.

steps.title: Time the endpoint switch
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Record which Pod `pg-cluster-rw` points at. Then, in one block in a single tab, capture the current endpoint, `kubectl delete pod <primary> --wait=false`, start the clock, and poll `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=pg-cluster-rw` once a second until the address changes; write the elapsed seconds to `/root/rw-switch-seconds.txt`. Compare it against `.status.targetPrimaryTimestamp` and `.status.currentPrimaryTimestamp`, then write through `pg-cluster-rw` and confirm the new primary served it. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The endpoint goes briefly empty before it changes — poll for a non-empty address that differs from the one you started with.

title: Primary Endpoint Switch in Under 20 Seconds
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy 3-instance CloudNativePG cluster with the cnpg plugin installed. Record where the write endpoint points, hand the primary role across while timing how long the endpoint takes to follow, and check your stopwatch against the operator's own promotion timestamps.
lectureNotes:
The claim being tested, and why it is looser than a failover's

CloudNativePG's end-to-end suite asserts two separate budgets for the write endpoint following a change of primary: under ten seconds after an unplanned failover, and under twenty after a planned switchover. It is worth understanding why the planned operation is allowed to be slower, because the reason is the same one that makes it safe.

A failover happens when the primary is already gone. There is nothing to shut down and nothing to wait for — the operator detects the loss, promotes a replica and moves the label. A switchover starts from a primary that is alive and serving, and deliberately shuts it down cleanly first: it stops accepting connections, flushes what it holds, and only then is the chosen replica promoted, having replayed the last of that WAL. That graceful shutdown is time a crash never spends, and it is exactly what makes a switchover lossless where a failover can only promise what replication had already delivered.

What you are actually measuring

Not the promotion, and not the operator's reaction time — the interval a client experiences. The `-rw` Service selects on the `cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary` label, so the endpoint moves when the operator moves that label onto the promoted instance. Between the old primary being demoted and the new one being labelled, the write endpoint is briefly empty rather than stale, which is how Kubernetes stops traffic reaching a database with no primary.

The measurement has to start at the request, in the same shell, with no human in the loop. `kubectl cnpg promote` returns immediately — it sets the cluster's target primary and the operator reconciles toward it — so the clock starts on the request rather than on its completion, and a one-second poll of the endpoint is precise enough for a twenty-second budget.

The cluster's own stopwatch

There is a second measurement that depends on nobody timing anything. The Cluster status carries `targetPrimaryTimestamp`, stamped when the operator decided there should be a new primary, and `currentPrimaryTimestamp`, stamped when that instance actually became one. The gap between them is the promotion itself; the difference between that and what you measured is the old primary's shutdown plus the endpoint update. Those two stamps are also how this lab is graded, so the claim is checked against the cluster's own record rather than against a number a learner typed.

steps.title: Time the endpoint switch
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Record which Pod `pg-cluster-rw` points at. Then, in one block in a single tab, capture the current endpoint, run `kubectl cnpg promote pg-cluster <replica>`, start the clock, and poll `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=pg-cluster-rw` once a second until the address changes; write the elapsed seconds to `/root/switchover-seconds.txt`. Compare against `.status.targetPrimaryTimestamp` and `.status.currentPrimaryTimestamp`, then write through `pg-cluster-rw` and confirm the promoted instance served it. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: Promote one of the two replicas — the argument order is `kubectl cnpg promote <cluster> <instance>`.

title: Recovering from a Degraded State
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy 3-instance CloudNativePG cluster. Destroy a replica, time how long the operator takes to restore three of three ready, and prove that what you watched was a rebuild and not a failover — same primary, same timeline, no promotion.
lectureNotes:
Degraded is not failed

A cluster that has lost a replica is degraded: it is short of the redundancy it was asked for, and it is still completely functional. There is a primary, it takes writes, the `-rw` Service never moves, and clients notice nothing. The distinction matters because the correct response is different. Losing the primary demands a promotion; losing a replica demands only that the missing instance be replaced, and a system that answered both with a failover would be far more disruptive than one that promotes only when it must.

CloudNativePG reports this in its own words. `kubectl get cluster` shows READY drop to 2 of 3 while STATUS reads "Waiting for the instances to become active", and returns to "Cluster in healthy state" when the replacement is streaming. In a real run on this environment the status caught up within about two seconds of the deletion and the cluster was healthy again roughly fifteen seconds later, against an end-to-end budget of sixty.

Why it is fast

Because almost nothing has to be copied. Deleting a Pod does not delete its PersistentVolumeClaim, so the replacement Pod reattaches to the same volume, with the same data directory it had a moment ago, and only has to replay the WAL it missed while it was gone. This is the same property that makes rolling restarts cheap, and it is worth contrasting with what happens when the *storage* is destroyed instead: then the instance has to be re-cloned from the primary in full.

Measuring it honestly

The timing loop has to wait for the cluster to actually report degraded before it starts looking for recovery. Kubernetes is eventually consistent, and the Cluster status takes a moment to catch up with a deletion that has already happened — a naive loop that polls once and sees three ready would report a recovery time of zero seconds, having measured nothing at all.

The proof that no failover happened

Two facts, both read from the cluster rather than assumed. `status.currentPrimary` is the same instance it was before, and `status.timelineID` is unchanged. A promotion always starts a new timeline, so an unchanged timeline is positive evidence that leadership never moved — much stronger than the absence of anything alarming in the logs.

steps.title: Destroy a replica and time the recovery
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Confirm 3/3 ready and both replicas streaming, write a row noted 'before-degradation', and record which replica you will delete. Then, in one block, delete it and poll `.status.readyInstances` and `.status.phase` until the cluster reports degraded and then healthy again, writing the elapsed seconds to `/root/recovery-seconds.txt`. Confirm `status.currentPrimary` and `status.timelineID` are unchanged, and that the row survived on all 3 instances. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: Delete a replica, not the primary — and let the loop wait for READY to drop before it starts looking for the recovery.

title: PVC Deletion
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy 3-instance CloudNativePG cluster. Delete a replica's PersistentVolumeClaim, find out why nothing happens, release it, and watch the operator provision fresh storage and re-clone the instance from the primary.
lectureNotes:
Deleting a claim in use does nothing, on purpose

`kubectl delete pvc` on a claim a running Pod is mounting reports success and then appears to do nothing. The claim enters `Terminating` — a deletion timestamp is set — and stays there indefinitely, while the database carries on without noticing. The reason is a finalizer, `kubernetes.io/pvc-protection`, which Kubernetes attaches to every claim: the object cannot be removed while a Pod still references it. This is deliberate protection against exactly the accident it looks like, and it is visible in `kubectl get pvc <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}'`.

Deleting the Pod is what releases it. Only then does the deletion complete, and with it the underlying PersistentVolume and the data on it.

What the operator does next

CloudNativePG's control loop wants the number of instances the Cluster asks for. With the claim and the Pod both gone, it provisions a new claim — same name, because instance claims are named after their instance — which binds to an entirely **new** PersistentVolume with a different uuid, and then re-clones the instance from the primary. That clone is a real base backup over the network, not a reattach, which is why it takes appreciably longer than replacing a Pod whose storage survived.

That difference is the whole lesson, and it is why the volume name is worth recording before starting. A claim that comes back with the same name proves nothing: claims are named after their instance and will always reappear. The `pvc-<uuid>` volume name is the identity of the actual storage, and a different uuid is what distinguishes "the data was rebuilt" from "the data was reattached".

What does not happen

No promotion. Destroying a replica's storage is not a reason to change leadership, so `status.currentPrimary` and `status.timelineID` are unchanged throughout, and writes continue against the same primary the entire time. The rebuilt instance ends up holding rows it never received as a running replica — it copied them from the primary during the clone, which is the clearest possible demonstration that its data came from somewhere else entirely.

steps.title: Destroy a claim and watch the rebuild
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Record a replica's volume name from `kubectl get pvc -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}'` and write a row noted 'before-pvc-deletion'. Delete that PVC and observe it stuck in `Terminating` with the `kubernetes.io/pvc-protection` finalizer, then delete the Pod to release it. Watch a new claim bind to a different volume and the instance re-clone from the primary, then confirm the row is present on it and that the primary never changed. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The claim's name comes back identical — it is the `pvc-<uuid>` VOLUME that tells you whether the storage is new.

title: Corrupted PVC
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running a healthy 3-instance CloudNativePG cluster, with the cnpg plugin installed. Find a replica's data directory on the node that holds it, fence the instance, destroy its control file, and read PostgreSQL's own refusal to open a database it cannot trust — then repair it the only way corruption can be repaired.
lectureNotes:
Where the data actually is

On a k3s cluster the bundled `local-path` StorageClass provisions a directory on a node, under `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/storage/<volume>_<namespace>_<claim>`. An instance's PostgreSQL data directory is therefore an ordinary directory on an ordinary filesystem, reachable by anything with root on that node — `PG_VERSION`, `base`, `global`, `pg_wal` and the rest, exactly as `initdb` laid them out. Seeing that once is worth a great deal of abstraction: a PersistentVolume is not a special object, it is a path.

Why corruption has to be done with the instance stopped

Overwriting files under a running PostgreSQL achieves less than it appears to. The control file in particular is rewritten on every checkpoint and on a clean shutdown, so damage done to a running instance is quietly undone the moment its Pod restarts. Fencing solves this: `kubectl cnpg fencing on` stops the PostgreSQL process while leaving the Pod running, so the files sit on disk with nothing to repair or rewrite them. Unfencing starts PostgreSQL again — this time against whatever is really there.

What PostgreSQL does about it

`global/pg_control` is a single 8 KB file recording the state of the entire cluster: the last checkpoint, the timeline, the WAL segment size, and a CRC over the whole thing. PostgreSQL reads it before it will open any database, and it will not guess. With the file overwritten, `pg_controldata` reports `calculated CRC checksum does not match value stored in control file`, and the postmaster exits with `FATAL: database files are incompatible with server` — having read a version number out of the noise and found it implausible.

The Pod stays `Running` while its container reports `0/1`: the instance manager is alive and retrying, PostgreSQL is not. The Cluster reports 2 of 3 ready, and the other two instances — including the primary — are completely unaffected.

The only repair

There is none, for the damaged copy. Restarting the Pod reattaches it to the same volume and reproduces the same failure. In a replicated database the answer is not to salvage the corrupt copy but to discard it: delete the claim and the Pod, let the operator provision fresh storage and re-clone the instance from a copy that is known good. The rebuilt instance comes back on a different volume with the data intact, and the cluster returns to three of three — with the primary never having been involved.

steps.title: Corrupt a data directory and repair it
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Write a row noted 'before-corruption', then find a replica's data directory under `/var/lib/rancher/k3s/storage/` on the node running it and record the path. Fence the instance with `kubectl cnpg fencing on pg-cluster <instance>`, overwrite `global/pg_control` with `dd if=/dev/urandom ... conv=notrunc`, and unfence it. Confirm the Pod goes 0/1, READY drops to 2, and the log shows the CRC mismatch. Repair by deleting the PVC and the Pod, and confirm the rebuilt instance is on a new volume with the row intact. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: Fence before corrupting — a running instance rewrites `pg_control` on shutdown and would undo the damage.

title: Backup and Restore from Volume Snapshots
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a real snapshot-capable CSI driver — k3s's own local-path cannot snapshot at all — and a PostgreSQL cluster sitting on it. Snapshot the volume, change the database afterwards, restore the snapshot into a new cluster beside the original, and find exactly one of the two rows in the copy.
lectureNotes:
Snapshots are a storage feature, not a database one

A volume snapshot is taken by the storage layer, through the CSI driver, and PostgreSQL is barely involved: the operator puts the database into backup mode, asks Kubernetes for a `VolumeSnapshot` of the instance's claim, and takes it out again. That makes it dramatically faster than a base backup — no copying gigabytes through a client — and it makes it entirely dependent on what your storage can do.

Most of the time in a lab environment, the answer is nothing. k3s ships `local-path`, which has no CSI driver behind it and cannot snapshot at all, so this environment installs the VolumeSnapshot API (three CRDs plus the snapshot-controller, none of which k3s provides) and a CSI driver that implements it.

One ordering rule matters more than it looks: CloudNativePG decides whether it supports volume-snapshot backups by checking for the VolumeSnapshot CRD *when the operator starts*. Install the API after the operator and every such backup is rejected with "Cannot use volumeSnapshot backup method due to missing VolumeSnapshot CRD... please restart it". This environment installs the snapshot stack first for exactly that reason.

What the backup produces

The same `Backup` resource as any other method, with `method: volumeSnapshot` — but what it leaves behind is a `VolumeSnapshot` object, owned by the storage layer, whose `readyToUse` field turns true when the driver has finished. Nothing can be restored from a snapshot before that. With `online: true` the snapshot is taken hot: PostgreSQL stays up and is put into backup mode for the duration, rather than being fenced and shut down.

Restoring creates a second cluster

This is the part that surprises people. A restore does not rewind the existing cluster; it creates a new one whose storage is cloned from the snapshot, using `bootstrap.recovery.volumeSnapshots`. The original keeps serving, untouched, while the copy comes up beside it with its own Pod, its own claim, its own `-rw`/`-ro`/`-r` Services and its own generated credentials. Pointing an application at the restored database means pointing it at the new cluster's Service.

The proof is in the claim and in the data. A restored instance's PersistentVolumeClaim carries a `dataSource` naming the VolumeSnapshot it was cloned from, where an ordinary claim has none. And a row committed to the original *after* the snapshot was taken is simply absent from the copy — which is not a fault but the definition of a snapshot: a copy of one instant, with everything after it living only in the cluster that kept running.

steps.title: Snapshot, change, restore, compare
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Compare `kubectl get storageclass` and `kubectl get volumesnapshotclass` to see what makes snapshots possible, and write a row noted 'before-snapshot'. Apply `/root/snapshot-backup.yaml`, wait for the Backup to complete and the VolumeSnapshot to report `readyToUse`, then write a second row noted 'after-snapshot'. Apply `/root/restored-cluster.yaml`, confirm the restored claim carries a `dataSource` naming the snapshot, and compare the two databases — the copy holds only the first row. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: A restore creates a second cluster beside the original; it never rewinds the one that is running.

title: Backups and Scheduled Backups on Object Storage
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a real S3-compatible object store beside it, the Barman Cloud plugin installed, and a PostgreSQL cluster with no backups of any kind. Describe the store to CloudNativePG, turn on continuous WAL archiving, take a backup that really lands in the bucket, and put backups on a schedule.
lectureNotes:
Backups moved out of the operator

CloudNativePG used to configure object-store backups directly in the Cluster, under `spec.backup.barmanObjectStore`. That field still exists in 1.30 and the API server answers every use of it with a deprecation warning: native Barman Cloud support is removed in 1.31, and clusters are expected to move to the Barman Cloud Plugin. This lab teaches the plugin, because the alternative is teaching something with a removal date on it.

The plugin is a separate deployment that the operator talks to over the CNPG-I plugin interface, and it authenticates with certificates — which is why cert-manager is a prerequisite, and why the plugin's manifest contains Certificate and Issuer resources rather than a static secret.

Three resources, three jobs

An `ObjectStore` describes a destination: the bucket, the endpoint, the credentials to use (by reference to a Secret, never inline), the retention policy and the WAL compression. It is inert on its own — creating one backs nothing up.

The Cluster then declares the plugin in `spec.plugins` with `isWALArchiver: true` and a `barmanObjectName` pointing at that store. This is a real change to the instances, so the operator rolls them; when it settles, PostgreSQL is archiving every completed WAL segment to the bucket. The `ContinuousArchiving` condition on the Cluster turns True only once a WAL file has actually arrived, so it is a statement about the bucket rather than about the configuration.

A `Backup` is a request for a base backup, with `method: plugin`. The operator carries it out and records where it wrote and which WAL range it covers — `beginWal` and `endWal` are the link between the base backup and the archive, because recovery means restoring the base and then replaying WAL from where it ends. A `ScheduledBackup` creates those requests on a cron schedule, in six fields starting with seconds, and each firing produces an ordinary Backup owned by the schedule.

Why both halves matter

A base backup alone restores you to the moment it was taken. The WAL archive alone has no starting point to replay onto. Together they define a recovery window, which `kubectl cnpg status` reports as "First Point of Recoverability" and "Last Successful Backup" — the two fields worth watching, because they are the honest answer to what you can and cannot recover to. The same command reports "Working WAL archiving" and how many segments are waiting, which is the early warning that a bucket has become unreachable long before anyone tries to restore from it.

steps.title: Archive, back up, schedule
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Create the credentials Secret and apply `/root/objectstore.yaml`, then declare the plugin on the Cluster with `isWALArchiver: true` and `barmanObjectName: seaweedfs-store`. Wait for the rollout, confirm `ContinuousArchiving=True` and check `kubectl cnpg status pg-cluster`. Apply `/root/backup.yaml` and wait for phase `completed`, then apply `/root/scheduledbackup.yaml` and wait for the schedule to fire. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The Secret's key names must match what the ObjectStore references — read them out of the staged manifest.

title: Restoring from Object Storage
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a real S3-compatible object store beside it, a PostgreSQL cluster already archiving WAL there, and a base backup already taken. Write a row after that backup, recover a second cluster from the bucket, and find your row in it — proof that recovery replays WAL rather than just unpacking a backup.
lectureNotes:
A restore is a new cluster, not a rewind

CloudNativePG does not restore into an existing cluster. Recovery is a *bootstrap method*: you create a new Cluster whose `bootstrap` section says `recovery` instead of `initdb`, and the operator assembles its database from an object store before starting PostgreSQL on it. The original keeps running, untouched, throughout — which is what makes a restore safe to attempt during an incident, and what means the end of a restore is a second database with its own Services and its own credentials, not a repaired first one.

Where the recovery reads from

Two blocks do the work. `bootstrap.recovery.source` names an entry in `externalClusters`, and that entry is where the Barman Cloud plugin is named along with the ObjectStore to read and, importantly, a `serverName`. One bucket routinely holds several clusters' backups, so the recovery has to say whose data it wants; `serverName` is the source cluster's name, and getting it wrong produces a recovery that finds nothing rather than an error at apply time.

Base backup plus WAL, not base backup alone

The part worth internalising is that a base backup is only a starting point. Recovery restores it and then replays the WAL archive forward from where the backup ended, which is why continuous archiving matters as much as the backups do — and why a cluster with backups but broken archiving can only ever recover to the moment of its last base backup.

The cheapest way to see this is to commit something *after* a base backup was taken and then recover: the row appears in the restored database, and it can only have come from the archive. `kubectl cnpg status` reports the two ends of that window as "First Point of Recoverability" and "Last Successful Backup", and "Working WAL archiving: OK" is the operator's statement that the second half of the mechanism is actually functioning.

What recovery looks like while it runs

A Job appears first — it fetches the base backup and replays WAL — and disappears when it is done, after which the instance Pod starts on the volume it produced. A recovery that takes minutes is usually replaying a long WAL archive, not stuck.

steps.title: Recover from the bucket
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Confirm the archive is working with `kubectl cnpg status pg-cluster` and `ContinuousArchiving=True`, then write a row noted 'after-backup' and force a WAL switch. Apply `/root/restore.yaml`, which bootstraps a new cluster with `bootstrap.recovery.source` and an `externalClusters` entry naming the barman-cloud plugin, the ObjectStore and `serverName: pg-cluster`. When it reports healthy, read the restored database and find the row the base backup never contained. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: `serverName` says whose backups to read out of the bucket — it is the source cluster's name.

title: Point-in-Time Recovery
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a real object store, continuous WAL archiving and a base backup already taken. Make two changes seconds apart, note the moment between them, and recover a cluster to exactly that moment — landing with the first change present and the second one gone.
lectureNotes:
Recovering to a moment, not to a backup

Point-in-time recovery is ordinary recovery with a stopping condition. The base backup is restored, WAL is replayed forward from it, and replay halts as soon as it reaches the target — everything committed after that instant is left in the archive, unapplied. That is what makes PITR the tool for undoing a mistake: you recover to just before the bad transaction, rather than to the last backup (losing everything since) or to now (keeping the mistake).

The target is declared as `bootstrap.recovery.recoveryTarget`, most usefully as `targetTime`. CloudNativePG also accepts targets expressed as an LSN, a transaction id, or a named restore point, and `targetImmediate` to stop as soon as the restored backup is consistent.

Where the timestamp should come from

From PostgreSQL, not from the shell. `SELECT now()` prints exactly the form a recovery target accepts — `2026-08-15 11:13:31.110651+00` — and it is the same clock the commit timestamps in the WAL were written against. A timestamp taken from a node's `date` invites a timezone or clock-skew discrepancy in the one place where being a second out changes which transactions survive.

The timestamp also has to be in the right place. Recorded before the change you want to keep, the recovery lands too early; recorded after the change you want to discard, it lands too late. The useful discipline is to capture the moment between two known commits, which turns the result into a proof rather than a hope.

What you end up with

A second cluster, independent of the original, holding the database as it stood at the instant you named — while the original still holds everything, and the archive still holds the WAL that was not replayed. Nothing is destroyed by a point-in-time recovery; a different view of history is constructed alongside what already exists.

steps.title: Recover to a chosen instant
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Write a row noted 'first', capture `SELECT now()` into `/root/target-time.txt`, then write a row noted 'second' and force a WAL switch. Substitute your timestamp into the staged template with `sed "s/TARGET_TIME/$(cat /root/target-time.txt)/" /root/pitr.yaml.template > /root/pitr.yaml`, apply it, and when the recovered cluster reports healthy compare the two databases: the copy holds only the first row. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: Take the timestamp between the two inserts — before or after, and the recovery proves nothing.

title: WAL Restore: Sequential and Parallel
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with an object store, a base backup and a deliberately large WAL archive — roughly a hundred segments for a recovery to replay. Time a recovery as it is, switch on parallel WAL prefetching, time an identical recovery again, and confirm the faster one produced exactly the same database.
lectureNotes:
Recovery is mostly fetching

A base backup restores in a single operation. The WAL archive does not: PostgreSQL asks for one segment at a time through its `restore_command`, and each request is a separate round trip to the object store. With a hundred segments to replay, recovery spends most of its time waiting for the next 16 MB file to arrive rather than applying records — and that is before the archive is somewhere with real network latency.

This is why the size of a WAL archive, not the size of the database, is usually what decides how long a recovery takes. A cluster backed up hourly has an hour of WAL to replay; one whose last base backup was a week ago has a week of it.

What maxParallel changes

The Barman Cloud plugin's `wal.maxParallel` setting tells it to fetch several segments ahead of the replay instead of one at a time. The records applied and the order they are applied in do not change at all; what changes is how many fetches are in flight while PostgreSQL is busy with the segment it already has.

It is a property of the ObjectStore — the archive — rather than of any one cluster, so every recovery reading that store inherits it.

Measuring it honestly

The effect is real but its size depends on the machine, the archive and the distance to the object store, so the only defensible way to talk about it is to measure both. In this environment, over archives of 106 to 125 segments against a local object store, three sequential recoveries took 81, 72 and 91 seconds and three with `maxParallel: 8` took 61, 56 and 60 — around a third faster, reproducibly across separate clusters. On a busy host the gap narrows, which is worth knowing before quoting a number to anyone.

The timing has to start at the apply and run in one shell, and the comparison is only meaningful if nothing else is churning at the same time — a recovery timed while another cluster is still starting measures the host, not the setting.

Speed is not the only question

A faster recovery is worth nothing if it recovers less, so the pair of restores is worth comparing on content as well as duration: same base backup, same archive, same replay, identical row counts. `maxParallel` is a transport-level optimisation, and confirming that it changed the speed and not the result is the part that makes it safe to turn on.

steps.title: Time both, compare both
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Record `SELECT archived_count FROM pg_stat_archiver` and check the ObjectStore has no `maxParallel`. Apply `/root/restore-sequential.yaml` inside a timing loop and write the elapsed seconds to `/root/sequential-seconds.txt`. Then patch the ObjectStore with `maxParallel: 8`, apply `/root/restore-parallel.yaml` the same way into `/root/parallel-seconds.txt`, and compare. Finally count rows in the source and both restored clusters — all three should match. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: Time the parallel run when nothing else is starting up; a busy host measures itself, not the setting.

title: Anatomy of the Operator Deployment
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with the CloudNativePG operator installed and a database for it to manage. Take an inventory of what an installed operator actually consists of, read the admission webhooks every Cluster passes through, then switch the operator off and watch the API server refuse a Cluster because of it.
lectureNotes:
What an installed operator is

Surprisingly little. One namespace, `cnpg-system`, containing a single-replica Deployment, a Service on port 443, a ServiceAccount, and the RBAC binding it to a cluster-scoped ClusterRole. That one process watches every namespace in the cluster, which is why its permissions are cluster-scoped rather than namespaced.

Outside the namespace there are two more objects that matter as much as the Deployment: a MutatingWebhookConfiguration and a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration. Every Cluster, Backup, ScheduledBackup and Pooler you submit is intercepted by them before it is stored — the mutating one fills in defaults, the validating one can reject the request outright.

Why the webhook is load-bearing

Those configurations carry `failurePolicy: Fail`, which means that if the API server cannot reach the webhook it refuses the request rather than admitting it unvalidated. Scale the operator to zero and the webhook Service loses its only endpoint, and any attempt to create a Cluster is rejected with a message about failing to call the webhook and no endpoints being available.

That is worth provoking deliberately, because it is the error people meet by accident: install the operator, apply a Cluster immediately, and the apply fails because the operator Pod has not finished starting. Knowing the mechanism turns a confusing error into an obvious one — wait for the Pod, not for the CRDs.

Leader election, with one replica

The operator takes a Lease in its own namespace even though the default installation runs a single replica. The holder identity is the Pod name plus a random suffix, so it changes whenever the Pod is replaced. The Lease is what makes it safe to run more than one replica for availability: only the holder reconciles, and a replacement takes over by acquiring it.

None of this is on the data path. The operator's Pods, webhooks and Lease have nothing to do with a client connecting to PostgreSQL — which is why an operator that is scaled to zero costs repair, not availability.

steps.title: Inventory, webhooks, and the failure mode
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

List `kubectl -n cnpg-system get all` and record the operator Pod name. Read the validating webhook configuration — the resources it covers, the Service it calls and its `failurePolicy` — and record how many webhooks it defines. Then `kubectl -n cnpg-system scale deploy cnpg-controller-manager --replicas=0`, try `kubectl apply -f /root/cluster.yaml --dry-run=server`, capture the rejection, and scale the operator back up. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: `--dry-run=server` goes through admission without creating anything; capture stderr with `> file 2>&1`.

title: Configuring the Operator with a ConfigMap
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with the CloudNativePG operator running on defaults, because the ConfigMap it was told to read does not exist. Create it, ask for Cluster labels to be inherited by everything the operator generates, and discover that nothing happens until the operator is restarted.
lectureNotes:
Operator-wide settings live in one ConfigMap

Per-cluster settings go in the Cluster resource. Settings that apply to the operator itself go in a single ConfigMap in the operator's namespace, whose name is passed to the operator on its command line — the default installation starts it with `--config-map-name=cnpg-controller-manager-config` and `--secret-name=cnpg-controller-manager-config`, and neither object exists until someone creates it. A default installation is therefore an operator running with every operator-wide setting at its default, pointed at configuration that is not there.

What you can set there includes `INHERITED_LABELS` and `INHERITED_ANNOTATIONS` (keys whose values are copied from a Cluster onto every object generated from it), `MONITORING_QUERIES_CONFIGMAP`, certificate durations, and the namespaces to watch.

Read once, at startup

The detail that catches people is that the operator reads this ConfigMap when it starts, not continuously. Create or edit it and nothing changes: no error, no warning, no reconciliation. The ConfigMap sits there looking exactly right while the operator carries on with the configuration it loaded when it booted. Only a restart — `kubectl rollout restart` on the operator Deployment — makes the change take effect.

Restarting the operator is safe in a way worth stating plainly: it is not on the data path, so rolling it does not restart, disturb or interrupt any PostgreSQL instance. The database Pods keep their ages and their restart counts.

Inherited labels, and why they are the good demonstration

`INHERITED_LABELS` is the easiest of these settings to see working. Label a Cluster with one of the listed keys and the operator copies it onto the Pods, the PersistentVolumeClaims and the Services it generates — applied by reconciliation, without recreating anything. It is how ownership, cost-centre or environment labelling stays consistent across generated objects that nobody labels by hand. And because the effect is visible on a dozen objects at once, the difference between "configured" and "configured and restarted" is impossible to miss.

steps.title: Configure, fail, restart, succeed
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Read the operator's args to find the ConfigMap name it wants, then create `cnpg-controller-manager-config` in `cnpg-system` with `INHERITED_LABELS="team,environment"`. Label the Cluster `team=payments` and confirm with `kubectl get pods -L team` that nothing inherits it. Restart the operator with `kubectl -n cnpg-system rollout restart deploy cnpg-controller-manager`, then check the Pods and PVCs again. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The operator reads that ConfigMap only at startup — a restart is the whole point of the exercise.

title: Operator Pod Deletion
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with the CloudNativePG operator and a healthy database. Delete the operator's Pod and watch the database not care; then switch the operator off entirely, break something while it is gone, and find that nothing is repaired and the cluster is not even reporting the truth about itself.
lectureNotes:
The operator is not on the data path

A client connecting to PostgreSQL reaches a Service, which reaches a Pod, which runs PostgreSQL. The operator is nowhere in that path. Deleting its Pod therefore has no effect on queries in flight or on the instances themselves: the Deployment replaces the Pod, the new process acquires the leader-election Lease, and reconciliation resumes — while the database carries on without a pause and without restarting anything.

The Lease is the visible part of that handover. Its holder identity is the operator Pod's name plus a random suffix, so watching it change is watching one process hand control to another.

What you actually lose

Scaling the operator to zero makes the point properly. With no operator running, delete an instance Pod and nothing replaces it. The cluster keeps serving on the instances that remain — genuinely degraded, with one fewer replica streaming — and no controller exists to do anything about it.

The more interesting casualty is the truth. `kubectl get cluster` still reports three of three ready in a healthy state, because a resource's status is a report written by its controller, not an observation of reality. With the controller stopped, the status is frozen at its last word on the subject. This is a general Kubernetes lesson that CloudNativePG makes unusually easy to see: status is a claim by a controller, and a controller that is not running makes no claims and revises none.

What comes back

Scale the operator up and the missing instance is recreated within seconds, and the status starts telling the truth again. The repair is quick because only the Pod was ever deleted — its PersistentVolumeClaim was untouched, so the replacement reattaches to the same storage and catches up by replaying WAL rather than being cloned from scratch.

The summary worth carrying away: an operator outage costs you repair, not availability. A cluster without one keeps serving and stops healing.

steps.title: Delete it, switch it off, bring it back
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Note the lease holder, delete the operator Pod with `kubectl -n cnpg-system delete pod -l app.kubernetes.io/name=cloudnative-pg`, and confirm the database still answers and the lease holder changed. Then `scale deploy cnpg-controller-manager --replicas=0`, delete a replica Pod, and observe that nothing replaces it while `kubectl get cluster` still claims 3 ready. Scale back to 1 and watch the instance be recreated. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: Delete a replica, not the primary — with no operator running there is nothing to promote a successor.

title: Operator Pod Eviction
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with the CloudNativePG operator and a healthy database. Evict the operator through the API that node drains use and watch it be allowed, add a PodDisruptionBudget and watch the same request be refused, then make it evictable again without weakening the budget.
lectureNotes:
Eviction is a request, deletion is not

Deleting a Pod is unconditional: the API server records the deletion and the kubelet acts on it. Eviction is different — it is a request to the `pods/eviction` subresource which the API server may refuse, and the thing it consults before answering is any PodDisruptionBudget covering that Pod.

This matters because eviction is exactly what `kubectl drain` issues for every Pod on a node. Whether a drain completes, hangs, or needs `--force` is decided entirely by how the API server answers those eviction requests, so understanding the answer is how you predict a drain before running one on something that matters.

There is no `kubectl evict` verb; the request goes to the subresource directly, which `kubectl create --raw /api/v1/namespaces/<ns>/pods/<pod>/eviction -f -` will do. A permitted eviction answers `{"status":"Success","code":201}`.

The single-replica trap

A PodDisruptionBudget of `minAvailable: 1` over a Deployment running exactly one replica permits **zero** disruptions — keeping one available and taking one away cannot both be satisfied. The budget's own `ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS` column says 0, and every eviction is refused with `Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget` and HTTP 429.

The consequence is a node drain that never finishes, blocked on a Pod that has been protected into immobility. It is a common and confusing outage, and the confusion comes from the budget looking correct in isolation — the problem is the replica count, not the budget.

The fix is to give the budget something to spare. Scaling the operator to two replicas leaves the same `minAvailable: 1` satisfiable, `ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS` becomes 1, and the identical eviction request is accepted. Deleting the budget would also unblock the drain, but it removes the protection instead of satisfying it.

What the database does throughout

Nothing. The operator is not on the data path, so evicting it — permitted or refused — has no effect on any PostgreSQL instance: no restarts, no failover, no dropped connections.

steps.title: Evict, block, unblock
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

POST an Eviction for the operator Pod with `kubectl create --raw /api/v1/namespaces/cnpg-system/pods/$POD/eviction -f /tmp/evict.json` and capture the 201. Create a PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable: 1` selecting `app.kubernetes.io/name: cloudnative-pg`, confirm ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS is 0, and capture the `TooManyRequests` refusal. Scale the operator to 2 replicas, confirm the budget now allows a disruption, and evict successfully. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: Deletion ignores budgets entirely — that is why drains use eviction.

title: Upgrading the Operator
