description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running the previous CloudNativePG minor release, with a database it bootstrapped and the newer release staged on disk. Record what is running, apply the upgrade, and find out what it cost the databases — which is nothing.
lectureNotes:
Upgrading is applying the newer manifest

There is no separate upgrade procedure for CloudNativePG and no migration step to run: you apply the newer release manifest over the older one, with `--server-side`, and the same command that installs also upgrades. Server-side apply is what makes that work — it reconciles field ownership on the API server rather than diffing against a stored copy of the last applied configuration, which is also why the CRDs (far too large for a client-side apply's 256 KB annotation) can be updated in place.

An operator upgrade is an API upgrade

A minor release usually brings new API surface, and the CRDs are part of the manifest. Going from 1.29.2 to 1.30.0 takes the CloudNativePG CRD count from 10 to 11, the newcomer being `failoverquorums.postgresql.cnpg.io` — a 1.30 feature whose API has to exist before anything can use it. The CRDs are applied before the Deployment rolls, for that reason.

What it costs the databases

Nothing, for a minor upgrade. The operator is a control-plane component that is not on the data path, so replacing it does not restart, fail over or disturb any PostgreSQL instance. In a real run of this upgrade the instance Pods' ages kept climbing straight through it and their restart counts stayed at zero — the same containers before and after, serving the same connections.

That is worth confirming rather than assuming, and the way to confirm it is to record the ages and restart counts before starting. It is also the thing that makes minor operator upgrades routine rather than a scheduled maintenance window, and the reason to keep an eye on release notes for the rare upgrade that does require an instance rollout.

After the upgrade, a cluster created by the older operator is reconciled by the newer one with nothing migrated by hand — the quickest way to confirm that is to delete an instance Pod and watch the new operator rebuild it.

steps.title: Apply the newer release
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Record the running image with `kubectl -n cnpg-system get deploy cnpg-controller-manager -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'`, count the CRDs, note the instance ages and restart counts, and write a row noted 'before-upgrade'. Then `kubectl apply --server-side -f /root/cloudnative-pg/releases/cnpg-1.30.0.yaml`, confirm the image and CRD count changed, and check the instances were never restarted. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The RESTARTS column on the instance Pods is the evidence — it should still read 0.

title: Operator High Availability
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with the CloudNativePG operator and a healthy database. Scale the operator out, find which replica actually holds the leader-election Lease, destroy it and time the takeover, then confirm the followers really were idle.
lectureNotes:
Why more replicas do not mean more throughput

The operator is started with `--leader-elect` and takes a Lease in its own namespace even when only one replica is running. Scale it to three and all three run the same binary and watch the same API server, but only the holder of that Lease reconciles anything — the others sit waiting for it to expire or be released.

That is deliberate and necessary. Two controllers acting on the same Cluster would race each other: both deciding to promote a replica, both creating the same Pod, both writing conflicting status. Leader election makes running several replicas a redundancy measure rather than a parallelism one.

Reading the Lease

`kubectl -n cnpg-system get lease` shows the holder identity, which is the Pod name followed by an underscore and a UUID. The UUID identifies the *process*, so a restarted Pod with the same name is still a new holder — which is what makes the field useful for spotting flapping leadership rather than just Pod churn.

How fast the handover is

Fast, when the leader shuts down cleanly: it releases the Lease on the way out, so a standby can claim it immediately rather than waiting for it to expire. In a real run, deleting the Lease holder saw another replica take over in about two seconds. An abrupt loss — a node disappearing rather than a Pod being deleted — takes longer, because there is nobody to release the Lease and the standbys must wait out its duration.

Measuring that honestly needs one detail: during the handover the holder field is briefly empty, so a loop that accepts any value different from the old leader will report a takeover of zero seconds having measured nothing at all. Wait for a holder that is both non-empty and different.

What the followers are doing

Nothing, and their logs say so: the last line of a non-leader is an attempt to acquire the leader lease. That is the confirmation that scaling out has not introduced two controllers fighting over the same database — and the cluster keeps being reconciled throughout, by whichever replica currently holds the Lease.

steps.title: Scale out, kill the leader, time the takeover
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Scale the operator to 3 replicas and record the Lease holder from `kubectl -n cnpg-system get lease -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.holderIdentity}' | cut -d_ -f1`. Delete that Pod inside a timing loop that waits for a non-empty, different holder, and write the elapsed seconds to `/root/takeover-seconds.txt`. Then read a follower's log to confirm it is waiting for the Lease, and delete an instance Pod to confirm reconciliation still works. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The holder field is briefly empty mid-handover — require non-empty *and* different, or you measure nothing.

title: Metrics Collection
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster whose PostgreSQL instances are already exporting Prometheus metrics. Scrape one by hand, read values you can check against the database itself, then add a metric of your own — a SQL query in a ConfigMap that the operator turns into a series.
lectureNotes:
The endpoint exists before any monitoring does

Every CloudNativePG instance Pod listens on port 9187 and serves `/metrics` in Prometheus exposition format, whether or not anything is scraping it. There is no ServiceMonitor to install and no exporter sidecar to add — so the first step in debugging a monitoring problem is to fetch the endpoint by hand and see what is actually there. From a k3s node's shell you can route straight to a Pod address, which makes that a single `wget` with no port-forward.

A healthy instance serves a few hundred `cnpg_` series before any customisation.

Check the collector before you trust the collection

`cnpg_collector_up` and `cnpg_collector_last_collection_error` describe the exporter itself. This is the pair to alert on first: if the exporter cannot reach PostgreSQL you get stale values rather than an obvious gap, and a dashboard full of numbers with `collector_up 0` behind it is worse than no dashboard.

Values you can verify

The useful discipline with any metric is to tie it back to something observable another way. `cnpg_backends_total` carries a `usename` label, so the backends connected as `streaming_replica` should number one per replica; `cnpg_pg_replication_slots_active` should likewise show one slot per replica. Both can be confirmed directly from `pg_stat_replication` and `pg_replication_slots` — the metrics are a projection of those views, which is exactly why a slot going inactive is worth alerting on.

Metrics about your data, not just about PostgreSQL

The built-in metrics describe the database engine. Anything about the application — queue depth, unprocessed rows, tenants over quota — has to come from a query you supply. CloudNativePG takes those as SQL in a ConfigMap: a metric family name, the query, and a description of each returned column with its type. The Cluster references the ConfigMap under `spec.monitoring.customQueriesConfigMap`, and the operator runs the query on the collection interval and exports the result as `cnpg_<family>_<column>`, carrying the description you wrote as its HELP text.

Because the metric *is* the query, its value and the database always agree — which makes it easy to verify and, in production, easy to reason about when it is wrong.

steps.title: Scrape, verify, extend
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Find the metrics port with `kubectl get pod pg-cluster-1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].ports[*]}'`, take the Pod IP and `wget -qO- http://$IP:9187/metrics`. Check `cnpg_collector_up`, count the `cnpg_` series, and confirm `cnpg_backends_total` and `cnpg_pg_replication_slots_active` against `pg_stat_replication`. Then create a ConfigMap with a custom query, reference it under `spec.monitoring.customQueriesConfigMap`, and watch `cnpg_lab_rows_total` appear and track the database. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: Run wget from the node — the PostgreSQL image has neither curl nor wget.

title: PgBouncer Metrics
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a PostgreSQL cluster and a Pooler left for you to create. Create it, scrape the metrics its PgBouncer Pods export, then send real traffic through it and watch a pool appear in the metrics that was not there before.
lectureNotes:
A different port, the same idea

PgBouncer Pods created from a Pooler export Prometheus metrics on port **9127** — not the 9187 a database instance uses. A scrape configuration that assumes one port silently collects nothing from the other, which is a common and quiet gap. Every series is prefixed `cnpg_pgbouncer_`, so one Prometheus job can scrape instances and poolers together and still tell them apart.

Each PgBouncer Pod exports only its own view. There is no aggregate endpoint, so a real scrape collects from every Pod and sums where it needs to — and a Pooler with two replicas will show a given pool on whichever Pod has actually served it.

What the series describe

Two families. The `lists_` counters are process-wide: how many databases, users and pools PgBouncer knows about, plus DNS bookkeeping. The `pools_` gauges are per database and user, and they are where the pooling story is told: `cl_active` and `cl_waiting` count client connections, `sv_active` and `sv_idle` count the server connections behind them, and `maxwait` is how long the longest-waiting client has been queued. The gap between the `cl_` and `sv_` numbers is the pooling you are getting; a rising `maxwait` is the signal that the pool is too small.

`cnpg_pgbouncer_last_collection_error` describes the exporter itself, which reaches PgBouncer's admin console to collect. Check it before trusting anything below it.

Pools appear when they are used

The detail that catches people writing alerts: PgBouncer reports pools it has actually served, not pools it has been configured to allow. Before any client connects, the only pool is PgBouncer's own admin database — the `database="app"` series simply does not exist. An alert written against a pool that has never carried traffic will never fire, because there is no series to evaluate.

Sending a few connections through the pooler's Service and watching the app pool appear is the cheapest way to internalise that, and it is worth doing before relying on any pool-level alert.

steps.title: Create, scrape, correlate
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Apply `/root/pooler.yaml` and wait for two PgBouncer Pods. Find the metrics port (9127) and scrape a Pod IP with wget from the node; check `cnpg_pgbouncer_last_collection_error` and count the `cnpg_pgbouncer_` series. Then connect through `pg-cluster-pooler-rw` a few times, write a row noted 'via-pooler', and scrape both Pods again to find the `database="app"` pool series that was not there before. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: The pooler Service load-balances, so scrape both PgBouncer Pods — a pool appears only on the one that served the traffic.

title: JSON Log Format
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster whose instances and operator log structured JSON by default. Take the format apart, provoke a real database error and find it by its SQLSTATE rather than its message, then collect one stream of logs across all three instances.
lectureNotes:
Structured by default, with no plain-text mode

CloudNativePG logs JSON to stdout and there is nothing to configure to get it. Every line — from the instance manager, from PostgreSQL, from the operator itself — shares one envelope: `level`, `ts`, `logger`, `msg` and `logging_pod`. A collector can index every line the same way regardless of which subsystem produced it, and the `logger` field is what tells them apart. Typical values on an instance are `postgres`, `instance-manager`, `pg_controldata` and `cluster-resource`.

PostgreSQL's own log arrives as data, not text

This is the part worth appreciating. PostgreSQL log lines are nested under a `record` key carrying its full CSV log field set as structured fields: `user_name`, `database_name`, `connection_from` with the client's address and port, `application_name`, `backend_type`, the `query` that ran, `error_severity` and `sql_state_code`.

None of it has to be parsed out of a message. A failing statement produces a record with `error_severity: ERROR` and a five-character SQLSTATE — `22012` for division by zero — and searching by that code finds every occurrence of that class of failure regardless of how the message is worded or which locale the server runs in. That is what you want in an alert; grepping for message text is what you fall back to when logs are unstructured.

One cluster, three logs

`kubectl logs` reads one Pod, and a cluster has three — with the interesting lines spread across all of them precisely when something is going wrong. The cnpg plugin's `logs cluster` subcommand collects them into a single stream, writes it to a file with `-o`, and with `-f` follows Pods that are created or recreated while it runs, which is what makes it usable during a failover.

The merge loses nothing, because each line still carries its own `logging_pod`: the combined stream can be split back apart or filtered to one instance, and filtering by `logger` across the whole cluster at once becomes a single grep instead of three interleaved commands.

Worth knowing about the tooling: neither the k3s nodes nor the PostgreSQL image ships `jq`, so field extraction in this environment is `grep -o '"field":"[^"]*"'` — which is enough for everything above.

steps.title: Read the structure, find an error, aggregate
steps.instructions:
Open a terminal on any of the 3 k3d nodes.

Read one line with `kubectl logs pg-cluster-1 --tail=1`, then list the distinct loggers with `grep -o '"logger":"[^"]*"' | sort -u` and record them. Run `SELECT 1/0;` through psql-client, find the resulting record in the primary's log and record its `sql_state_code`. Then collect every instance's log into one file with `kubectl cnpg logs cluster pg-cluster --tail 40 -o /root/all-pods.txt` and confirm all three Pods appear. Click Check Work.
steps.hint: No jq is installed anywhere here — `grep -o '"sql_state_code":"[0-9A-Z]*"'` is the extraction tool.

title: Replication Slots
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster whose replication slots already exist — CloudNativePG manages them by default. Find them, take a standby away and prove its slot is what lets it rejoin by catching up rather than being rebuilt, then turn the feature off and see exactly what the cluster loses.
lectureNotes:
Slots you did not create

A replication slot is how a standby tells a primary "do not recycle WAL I have not read yet". Without one, a primary trims WAL on its own schedule, and a standby that falls far enough behind can never catch up — it has to be rebuilt from a fresh base backup.

CloudNativePG manages these for you and switches them on by default. A healthy three-instance cluster already carries two physical slots named with a _cnpg_ prefix, one per replica, and nobody configured them. The operator also keeps matching slots on the standbys, so that whichever instance is promoted already holds the slots the others will need — that is what highAvailability means in this context.

The column that matters is restart_lsn: the oldest WAL position the slot still needs. The primary will not recycle past it, which is the entire mechanism.

What a slot is not

A slot does not carry data. Streaming replication works perfectly well without one, which is easy to prove by turning slots off and watching the cluster stay healthy. What the slot adds is a guarantee that applies only when a standby is disconnected: the WAL it still needs will be kept.

So the trade is disk against certainty. Slots cost you WAL that cannot be recycled while a standby is behind, and buy you the certainty that a standby returning late can still catch up rather than needing a rebuild. Turning them off returns the disk and removes the certainty — invisibly, until the day it matters.

title: Synchronous Replication
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster replicating asynchronously. Turn on synchronous replication, then take a standby away and watch a write park itself in the SyncRep wait event where statement_timeout cannot rescue it — and finally choose the other side of the durability trade and watch the behaviour change.
lectureNotes:
A policy, not a list of servers

By default a CloudNativePG cluster is asynchronous: the primary confirms a commit once it has written WAL locally, and standbys catch up when they catch up. Lose the primary and anything the standbys had not yet received is gone.

Synchronous replication makes the primary wait for standbys to acknowledge before it reports a commit. CloudNativePG expresses this as method and number — how many acknowledgements, and whether they come from any standby or from a ranked list. You declare the policy; the operator generates PostgreSQL's synchronous_standby_names and keeps it correct as instances come and go.

Two details in that generated value surprise people. The primary appears in its own list, because any instance might be primary later and a primary never counts itself as a standby. And with method any the standbys report sync_state quorum rather than sync — they are a pool, and whichever answers first satisfies the requirement.

Durability against availability

Every promise about durability is also a promise about availability, in the opposite direction. dataDurability decides which one wins when the standbys you asked for are not there.

required, the default, means the rule is absolute: not enough standbys, no acknowledged commits. A write parks in the SyncRep wait event, and the detail that catches people out is that statement_timeout will not end that wait — the statement has finished executing, and what is outstanding is the commit acknowledgement.

preferred means the operator shrinks the generated list to the standbys that can actually answer, so writes continue and the guarantee quietly relaxes at exactly the moment things are already going wrong. Neither setting is the safe one; they are different definitions of safe.

title: Scaling a Cluster Up and Down
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a healthy 3-instance database. Change one integer and watch the operator clone a new instance from the primary — volume, slot and all — then prove it carries data written before it existed, and scale back down accounting for everything that gets removed.
lectureNotes:
One integer, four objects

Scaling a CloudNativePG cluster is editing spec.instances. Everything that follows is the operator's work: a PersistentVolumeClaim, a clone of the primary, a replication slot, and a Pod.

The clone is worth watching for. A short-lived join Pod appears first — the operator running pg_basebackup against the primary to build the new instance's data directory. Only once that exists can the instance start and begin streaming. This is why a new instance carries rows written before it existed, and why scaling up is quick on a small database and slow on a large one: the cost is copying the data directory, not replaying the database's history.

Scaling down removes the highest-numbered instance — not the newest, not the least busy, and you do not get to choose.

The bookkeeping that is invisible until it is not

Three things go when an instance goes: the Pod, its PersistentVolumeClaim, and its replication slot on the primary. The first is obvious and the other two are the ones worth checking.

The volume is deleted rather than orphaned, so scaling down really does return the storage. And the slot is dropped by the operator, which matters more than it sounds: a slot belonging to an instance that no longer exists would make the primary reserve WAL forever. The first symptom of that is a full volume, which looks nothing like a replication problem, and is why an operator tidying up after itself is worth confirming rather than assuming.

title: Replica Clusters
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a healthy source database and a staged manifest for a second one. Stand up a whole separate Cluster that streams from the first, prove it genuinely refuses writes, then detach it and watch it start a timeline of its own.
lectureNotes:
A separate Cluster, not another instance

Adding an instance to a cluster gives you one more Pod inside the same Cluster object, managed as a unit. A replica cluster is a different thing: its own Cluster object, its own name, its own Services and Secrets and lifecycle, which happens to be following another one. That is the shape used across namespaces, across Kubernetes clusters and across regions, and it is the basis of a disaster-recovery topology.

Two fields build it. bootstrap.pg_basebackup clones the source once to get a starting data directory, and replica.enabled keeps it a standby afterwards rather than letting it promote itself the moment the clone finishes. The connection is described by an externalClusters entry using the streaming_replica role with certificates from the source's own Secrets — no password anywhere, because the source authenticates the connection with a certificate it issued.

That entry connects to the postgres database, and it has to: the source's generated pg_hba.conf lets streaming_replica reach only that database and the replication pseudo-database. It is a role for shipping WAL, not for reading rows.

Read-only means read-only

From PostgreSQL's point of view the replica cluster is simply one more streaming standby, appearing in the source's pg_stat_replication under the cluster's name. Everything that makes it a cluster is on the Kubernetes side.

It refuses writes with a read-only transaction error, not a permissions error — the superuser is refused too, because the whole instance is in recovery. That distinction is worth checking rather than assuming: a replica cluster which quietly accepted writes would leave two databases diverging while both looked healthy.

Detaching is one field and is not reversible. Setting replica.enabled to false promotes the instance out of recovery and it becomes an ordinary writable database — on a new timeline. PostgreSQL numbers each lineage of a database's history and a promotion starts a new one, so the moment you detach, the two histories diverge and streaming can never merge them back.

title: Logical Replication
description: This lab builds you two real PostgreSQL clusters and nothing flowing between them. Set up logical replication declaratively — a Publication on one, a Subscription on the other, both as Kubernetes resources — and meet the privilege requirements that make logical replication fail quietly when they are not met.
lectureNotes:
Rows, not WAL blocks

Physical replication ships WAL and produces a byte-identical standby. Logical replication decodes WAL into row changes and sends those, so the subscriber is a fully writable database that happens to be receiving some tables. It can have different indexes, extra tables, even a different major version.

CloudNativePG makes both sides declarative: a Publication resource on the publisher and a Subscription resource on the subscriber, each of which the operator turns into the ordinary PostgreSQL object the equivalent SQL would have made. Both carry a status with an applied flag, and that flag is the only place a failure shows up.

wal_level is already logical — the CloudNativePG default — so unlike almost every other PostgreSQL deployment there is nothing to change and no restart to schedule.

The privileges, and the quiet failures

Because the subscriber connects as an ordinary client and reads your tables, it needs privileges a streaming standby never does, and each missing one fails differently.

The connecting role needs REPLICATION or the publisher refuses the connection outright. The certificate-authenticated streaming_replica role cannot be used for this at all: the source's pg_hba only admits it to the postgres database, and your tables are not there. So the role is a password role — typically app — with REPLICATION granted to it.

That role also needs SELECT on the published tables. Without it the subscription applies cleanly, reports itself healthy, and never copies a row; the only evidence is permission denied for table in the subscriber's log. A table created by the app role is readable by it automatically, which is why creating tables as your application role rather than as postgres avoids the problem entirely.

And the Subscription's publicationDBName has to name the database the publication actually lives in when the external cluster connects to a different one. Get that wrong and the subscription connects, applies, and does nothing — with publication does not exist appearing only as a warning in the log.

A subscription creates a logical slot on the publisher, which retains WAL exactly as a physical slot does. An abandoned subscription is therefore an operational hazard, not a tidy-up job.

title: Fencing an Instance
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a healthy 3-instance database. Fence one instance and work out precisely what stopped and what was left alone — the Pod stays, the volume stays, and only PostgreSQL is gone — then keep writing to the rest of the cluster and bring it back.
lectureNotes:
Stopped, not destroyed

Fencing stops PostgreSQL on an instance while leaving everything around it in place. It is not a delete, not a scale-down and not a drain, and the difference is the reason to use it: the data directory stays exactly as it was at the moment the server stopped.

That is the state you want before inspecting an instance you suspect is damaged, or when a suspect instance must stop answering queries immediately. Deleting the Pod would give you a fresh instance and destroy the evidence.

The interface is an annotation, cnpg.io/fencedInstances, carrying a JSON list of instance names. The plugin's fencing on and fencing off subcommands are a convenience over kubectl annotate, which is worth knowing when the plugin is not to hand.

What actually changes

The Pod keeps running with a restart count of zero, but its Ready condition goes false — which is what removes it from the Services, since endpoints only carry ready Pods. Inside the container only the instance manager process remains; there is no postgres process at all, and a psql over the Pod's own socket fails because the socket file is gone.

Unfencing reverses it. The instance manager starts PostgreSQL, it reconnects to the primary and replays the WAL it missed from the replication slot the cluster kept for it. No rebuild, no base backup, no manual resynchronisation.

The operational trap is that fencing is a decision the operator will not overrule. There is no timeout and no automatic failover out of it, so a cluster fenced by mistake — or a primary fenced without a plan — stays down until somebody removes the annotation.

title: Hibernating a Cluster
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a healthy 3-instance database. Hibernate it, account for exactly what is released and what is kept — no Pods, all three volumes — then wake it and prove nothing was lost.
lectureNotes:
Off, but not gone

A database nobody is using still costs what it costs. Hibernation shuts a cluster down without deleting it: the Pods go, the PersistentVolumeClaims stay, and the Cluster object remains as the record of what to bring back.

That combination distinguishes it from the two things it is easily confused with. Scaling to zero is not available — a CloudNativePG Cluster has no such setting. Deleting the Cluster would take the volumes with it, making the return trip a restore from backup rather than a resume.

As with fencing, the plugin sets an annotation — cnpg.io/hibernation — and the operator does the work. Hibernating removes every instance Pod while leaving all the volumes bound; the Services still exist but have no endpoints, so a connection has nowhere to go. A hibernated cluster is genuinely off, not idling.

The return trip

hibernate off recreates the Pods and attaches the volumes that were waiting. It is neither a restore nor a rebuild: the instances start on the data directories they already had, so the primary comes up on its own volume rather than being bootstrapped from anywhere. Expect around a minute for three instances.

The clearest way to see the mechanism is to compare ages afterwards. The Pods are seconds old and the PersistentVolumeClaims are as old as the cluster — new compute, old storage. That is the trade hibernation makes: you stop paying for CPU and memory and go on paying for disk, which is exactly the right shape for a staging database between releases or a review environment nobody is looking at.

title: PostgreSQL Configuration Changes
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running entirely on generated configuration. Change three parameters and meet the three different things that can happen: one takes effect on a reload, one forces a rolling restart of every instance, and one is refused outright by the admission webhook because it is the operator's to set.
lectureNotes:
Declared, not edited

PostgreSQL configuration under CloudNativePG lives in spec.postgresql.parameters. You change the Cluster and the operator writes postgresql.conf; editing that file by hand is pointless because it is reconciled away.

What a change costs depends entirely on the parameter, and there are three outcomes rather than two.

Reload-only parameters — most logging and planner settings — take effect immediately. PostgreSQL rereads its configuration, pg_settings.pending_restart stays false, and no container is touched.

Restart-required parameters, such as max_connections, are allocated at startup. pending_restart goes true and the operator rolls the cluster: replicas first, one at a time, primary last, keeping a working database available for as long as possible.

The detail worth knowing about that roll is what happens to the primary. With the default primaryUpdateMethod of restart, the primary's Pod is not recreated at all — the instance manager restarts PostgreSQL inside the running container, so the restart count stays at zero while pg_postmaster_start_time moves on. Setting switchover instead promotes a replica and demotes the primary: shorter write downtime, but the primary moves.

Some parameters are not yours to set

The third outcome is that nothing happens at all. Some parameters belong to the operator — the ones deciding how instances find each other, where the data lives, and what PostgreSQL loads at startup — and the admission webhook refuses the whole update before it is stored.

listen_addresses, data_directory, shared_preload_libraries and hot_standby all come back with Can't set fixed configuration parameter. A second flavour is more interesting: wal_log_hints: off is refused with must be set to `on` when `instances` > 1, which is the webhook reasoning about the cluster you actually have rather than applying a blanket ban — the same request would be allowed on a single-instance cluster.

This is a good failure: loud, immediate, specific about the field at fault, and it changes nothing, so there is nothing to undo.

The habit that follows: a configuration change is not done when the patch is accepted, or even when the cluster returns to healthy. It is done when you have read the value back out of pg_settings and seen what PostgreSQL is really running. The operator's own values live in custom.conf in the data directory, included from postgresql.conf — that is the file to read when the spec and the running value seem to disagree.

title: Rolling Updates on Image Changes
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster deliberately running a PostgreSQL minor release behind. Change one field, watch the operator roll the new image through the cluster instance by instance while the database keeps serving, and account for what it cost.
lectureNotes:
One field, every instance

Upgrading a PostgreSQL minor release under CloudNativePG is changing spec.imageName. The operator replaces the instances one at a time — replicas first, primary last — which is what keeps the database usable throughout: each replica is replaced while the primary keeps serving, and only at the end does the instance handling writes change.

There is a window where the spec names the new image and some Pods still run the old one. That mixed state is not a broken cluster, it is a roll in progress, and telling those apart at a glance is worth practising. It also explains why the image a Pod is *running* must be read from .status.containerStatuses[0].image rather than from its spec.

A minor release needs no data migration: the on-disk format is compatible, so an instance starts on the same data directory with a newer binary. The PersistentVolumeClaims are never touched, which is why the whole operation is cheap — new Pods, old storage.

Why this differs from a configuration change

An image change cannot be applied in place. A container must be recreated to run a different image, so every instance gets a new Pod — including the primary, whose PostgreSQL can merely be restarted inside its existing container when only parameters change.

Which leaves the choice of primaryUpdateMethod. The default, restart, recreates the primary's Pod last and keeps its role. switchover instead promotes an already-upgraded replica and demotes the old primary — less write downtime, at the cost of moving the primary. Worth deciding deliberately rather than discovering during a maintenance window.

None of this applies to a major version upgrade, which changes the on-disk format and is a different operation entirely.

title: Image Catalogs
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster naming its PostgreSQL image directly. Move it onto an ImageCatalog so the image comes from a shared object, then upgrade it by editing only that object — the Cluster is never touched.
lectureNotes:
An indirection, and what it buys

A Cluster can name its PostgreSQL image directly in spec.imageName, or point at an ImageCatalog with spec.imageCatalogRef and let the catalog decide. The two are mutually exclusive, so adopting a catalog means removing the direct name and adding the reference in one atomic patch.

An ImageCatalog is a lookup from PostgreSQL major version to container image. Its schema is easy to get wrong: spec.images is the required list and its entries are major and image, while spec.componentImages is a separate optional list keyed by key and image for non-PostgreSQL components such as PgBouncer. Putting major under componentImages is rejected outright with a strict-decoding error.

Adopting a catalog that names the image already running is a no-op — nothing rolls, and the Pod ages carry on climbing. That is the point: the indirection is introduced without a change in behaviour.

Upgrading from somewhere else

Once the reference is in place, changing which image the catalog maps major 18 to rolls every Cluster that references it, in the ordinary way — replicas first, primary last, every Pod recreated. The Cluster object is not edited at all, and afterwards its spec still names no image.

For one cluster that is a curiosity. For a fleet it is the whole point: upgrading fifty clusters is editing one object, and the clusters cannot drift from it because they have no image of their own to drift with. The same question — what is everything running — stops being a query across every Cluster and becomes a read of one.

ClusterImageCatalog is the cluster-scoped variant, identical in shape but not namespaced, for clusters spread across namespaces.

title: Hot Standby Sensitive Parameters
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running on generated configuration. Find the five settings a standby may not hold lower than its primary, discover the on-disk channel by which it learns the primary's values, and watch the operator roll a change in the only order that is safe.
lectureNotes:
Five settings with a rule attached

max_connections, max_worker_processes, max_wal_senders, max_prepared_transactions and max_locks_per_transaction govern fixed-size shared memory structures that recovery has to replay into. A standby must hold each of them at a value no lower than its primary's; one that does not cannot start hot standby, and refuses read connections naming the offending setting.

The interesting question is how a standby knows what the primary's values are. Not from its own configuration, and not by asking. PostgreSQL writes a parameter-change record into the WAL whenever one of these settings changes, and a standby replaying that record updates its control file. pg_controldata on a standby therefore reports the primary's values, not its own — the limits travel through the write-ahead log like everything else. Two of them are abbreviated there as max_prepared_xacts and max_locks_per_xact, which is a small trap when searching.

Why replicas roll first

When one of these changes, CloudNativePG rolls the standbys first and the primary last. For these settings that order is not a preference. Raising the primary first would leave the standbys below it, and the moment they replayed the parameter-change record they would refuse to serve reads. Doing the standbys first means they are already at the higher value when the primary arrives.

The order does not reverse for a decrease, even though lowering is the safe direction — one order is safe both ways, so there is nothing to gain from having two. The primary's Pod is not recreated either way: its postmaster restarts inside the running container under the default primaryUpdateMethod of restart.

Inside a CloudNativePG cluster you never hand-manage these, because one configuration is applied to every instance in a safe order. Where the rule bites is outside that — a standby built by hand, or a restore onto a machine configured more modestly than the primary it came from.

title: Replica Cluster from a Backup
description: This lab builds you a real object store with a real base backup already in it. Bring up a second cluster from that backup as a replica rather than a new primary, and prove the two databases are coupled only through the bucket — with no connection between them at all.
lectureNotes:
One field between a restore and a replica

Restoring from object storage normally produces a new, independent primary: it replays what is in the bucket, promotes itself and starts its own timeline. Setting replica.enabled changes that entirely — the recovered cluster stays in recovery when the restore finishes and goes on replaying whatever the source archives.

The manifest has three parts worth reading separately. bootstrap.recovery names the external cluster to restore from; replica.enabled with replica.source names the same external cluster to keep following; and externalClusters defines it through the Barman plugin as a bucket and a server name. There is no host, no port and no credential for the source cluster anywhere in the file, because none is needed.

Coupled through a bucket

That is the property that distinguishes this from a streaming replica cluster. Ask the source's pg_stat_replication who is replicating from it and the replica cluster is not there — it is not a client of the primary, it is a client of object storage.

The cost is latency measured in WAL segments rather than milliseconds: a row written on the source does not appear until the segment carrying it is archived, which is why pg_switch_wal makes the difference visible immediately in a lab. The benefit is that the replica needs no network path to the source at all, which is the whole reason to run one in another region.

The clearest single view of the difference is on the replica itself: a cluster fed by an archive has no WAL receiver, so pg_last_wal_receive_lsn stays empty while pg_last_wal_replay_lsn advances.

title: Replica Cluster from a Volume Snapshot
description: This lab builds you a real snapshot-capable CSI driver and a database on it. Snapshot a running database, grow a second cluster whose data directory is that snapshot, and have it follow the original by streaming — the snapshot as seed rather than as the whole story.
lectureNotes:
A copy that is not a copy

Cloning a database by copying files takes time proportional to its size. A volume snapshot does not: for a storage driver that supports it natively, a snapshot is a metadata operation that completes in about the same time whether the volume holds a megabyte or a terabyte.

k3s's default local-path class cannot snapshot at all, which is why this environment installs a real CSI driver and the external-snapshotter CRDs first. A VolumeSnapshot names a source PersistentVolumeClaim and a VolumeSnapshotClass and says nothing about PostgreSQL — the storage layer does not know the volume holds a database. Behind it sits a cluster-scoped VolumeSnapshotContent representing the actual snapshot, and readyToUse on the snapshot is what says the copy exists rather than merely the request for it.

Nothing quiesces the database first. The result is crash-consistent, exactly like pulling the power — which is usable precisely because recovering from a crash is something PostgreSQL does on every start.

Seed, then stream

A snapshot is a moment, not a stream, so bootstrapping from one alone leaves a cluster frozen at the instant it was taken. Pairing bootstrap.recovery.volumeSnapshots with replica.enabled and a streaming externalClusters entry fixes that: the snapshot supplies the starting point and streaming replication carries it forward.

That combination is the practical way to add a replica to a large database — seed in seconds from a snapshot, then catch up the small remainder over the wire, instead of streaming the entire database across the network.

Unlike a replica fed from an archive, this one has a WAL receiver, so pg_last_wal_receive_lsn advances alongside the replay position and new rows arrive in seconds rather than waiting for a segment to be archived.

title: Database Initialization with InitDB
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with the operator installed and no database at all. Bootstrap one with initdb options spelled out — database, owner, locale, checksums, WAL segment size and two SQL hooks — then discover that changing your mind afterwards is accepted and has no effect whatsoever.
lectureNotes:
What initdb decides

Every PostgreSQL cluster begins with initdb, and spec.bootstrap.initdb is where you say what it should do rather than accepting the defaults of an app database owned by an app role in UTF8.

Its fields fall into two groups. database, owner and encoding describe what to create. localeCollate, localeCType, dataChecksums and walSegmentSize are physical choices written into the structure of the data directory itself, readable afterwards from pg_settings and from pg_controldata.

Two of the fields are hooks rather than settings. postInitSQL runs statements in the postgres database as superuser; postInitApplicationSQL runs them inside the application database once it exists. Which one you use decides which database your objects land in, so a CREATE TABLE in postInitSQL creates it somewhere almost nobody wants it.

One reading is a trap: data_checksums is on even in a cluster that never asked, because PostgreSQL 18's own initdb enables checksums by default. CloudNativePG's dataChecksums controls whether -k is passed, so on 18 the setting you would actually have to reach for is the one that turns them off.

Bootstrap is an instruction, not desired state

This is what makes the section different from every other part of a Cluster. Change instances and the operator adds one; change imageName and it rolls. Change anything under bootstrap and nothing happens at all — it was carried out once, at creation, and is never consulted again.

The failure is silent. Patching database, walSegmentSize or dataChecksums on a running cluster is accepted by the API server with no webhook rejection, no warning and no condition. The spec simply becomes a permanent description of something untrue, and kubectl get cluster -o yaml will keep reporting it for the life of the cluster.

So get the block right before applying, because the only way to change encoding or collation afterwards is a dump and restore into a new cluster — not a replica. And when reading someone else's cluster, remember that for bootstrap the spec records what was once asked for; only the database can tell you what is actually there.

title: Taints and Tolerations
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with one database instance per node. Taint a node out of the scheduling pool, watch the instance already there carry on regardless, then delete it and find it stranded for two reasons at once — only one of which is the taint.
lectureNotes:
NoSchedule is about the future

A taint marks a node as unsuitable and the effect decides how strongly. NoSchedule refuses new placements and does nothing else — an instance already running on a freshly tainted node stays exactly where it is, and the database never notices. NoExecute is the effect that removes what is already there.

Reaching for a taint and expecting a node to drain is a common and expensive misunderstanding, and it is worth proving to yourself once: taint the node, look at the Pods, and find all of them still Running.

Two reasons a Pod will not schedule

The taint costs nothing until something needs placing. Delete the instance on a tainted node and the scheduler reports its reasoning in full: 0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 node(s) didn't match PersistentVolume's node affinity.

That second clause is the more interesting half. A local-path claim pins its instance to the node the volume was created on, recorded as the volume.kubernetes.io/selected-node annotation, so the Pod may only go to one node — and that is the node now tainted. Neither fact alone would strand it. Meanwhile the cluster is degraded rather than down: two of three ready, still taking writes.

The toleration is on the workload

A toleration under spec.affinity.tolerations is the workload's side of the conversation, and the operator writes it verbatim onto every instance Pod it creates. Declaring one schedules the stranded instance back onto the node it was always pinned to.

The check worth doing at the end is that the node is still tainted. Nothing about it changed; what changed is who is willing to run there. That is also the boundary of when the pattern is appropriate — tolerating a taint is right when a node is reserved for a purpose and your database is that purpose, and wrong when the taint means maintenance, where it amounts to insisting on running exactly where somebody said not to.

title: Node Selectors and Pod Anti-Affinity
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster whose three database instances are spread one per node by a rule you never wrote. Read that rule, confine the cluster to nodes you label yourself, and turn the operator's spreading preference into a hard requirement to find out what each of them refuses.
lectureNotes:
The rule you did not write

A Cluster manifest that says nothing about scheduling still gets sensible placement, because the operator's admission webhook defaults spec.affinity.podAntiAffinityType to preferred. Read the Cluster back and that single word is there; read a Pod and you find what it expands into — a preferred anti-affinity term with weight 100, selecting the other instances of the same cluster, measured across the topology key kubernetes.io/hostname.

The topology key is the part worth noticing, because it decides what spreading even means. Across hosts is a different promise from across racks or zones, and the key is not written in the Cluster spec until you override it.

A node selector is a hard filter, and it is stamped on the Pod

spec.affinity.nodeSelector is a set of labels a node must carry. There are no weights and no fallback: a node either matches or is not a candidate. The operator writes it onto every instance Pod it creates, which means changing it triggers a rolling update — the existing Pods do not match the Pods the operator would generate now.

On local-path storage that combination bites. An instance is pinned to the node holding its volume, so if that node lacks the label the Pod cannot be placed anywhere: the scheduler answers 0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match PersistentVolume's node affinity, 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector. The rollout then stops with the cluster short of one instance, because the operator will not take a second one away while it is degraded. Labelling the remaining nodes fixes it without touching the database — the requirement was satisfied rather than relaxed.

preferred and required differ only when it matters

With one node per instance the two settings behave identically, which is exactly why the difference is usually discovered during an incident. required means the scheduler refuses rather than compromises, and the refusal reads 1 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules.

The most common way to meet this in production is a required spread measured over a topology with a single domain — asking for one instance per zone in a single-zone cluster. Every instance beyond the first has nowhere to go. required is the honest choice when co-locating instances would defeat the point of having them, and it costs the ability to run on fewer nodes than you have instances; preferred keeps the database up through a node shortage and quietly gives up the spread. Neither is wrong, but picking one without knowing which is.

title: PodSpec Drift Detection
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a healthy database and has you look at how the operator decides a Pod needs replacing. Read the record it keeps on every Pod, change a field that has nothing to do with PostgreSQL and watch the cluster roll for it, then corrupt that record by hand to prove which side of the comparison is real.
lectureNotes:
The operator writes down what it generated

Every instance Pod carries an annotation, cnpg.io/podSpec, holding the complete Pod spec the operator produced when it created that Pod: volumes, probes, the instance manager's command line, the security context, a terminationGracePeriodSeconds of 1800. Reconciliation compares that record with a freshly generated spec, and a difference is drift.

Most of what is in the record never appears in the Cluster manifest. That is the point — the manifest is a description of a database, and the record is the Pod that description turned into.

Drift rolls the cluster, replicas first

A change to something as ordinary as spec.resources rolls every instance, because a container's resources cannot be changed without replacing the Pod. The operator takes the replicas one at a time and leaves the primary until last, so the cluster is never short of more than one instance.

What it does not do is hand the role to somebody else. The phase reads Primary instance is being restarted without a switchover, and the instance that was primary before is primary afterwards — in a new Pod, with a new creation timestamp and a restart count of zero, because the Pod was replaced rather than restarted. That distinction between a rolling update and a failover is worth holding on to.

The comparison is against the record, not the object

Overwrite one Pod's cnpg.io/podSpec annotation with nonsense and the operator deletes and rebuilds that Pod within a few seconds, then writes the real spec back. Nothing about the running container had changed; only the operator's record of it. Drift detection reads the annotation.

A label of your own on the same Pod, by contrast, is left alone indefinitely. The operator is not enforcing an identical copy of what it created — it enforces the record it keeps and the labels it routes on, and ignores everything else.

That is also the explanation for one of the nastier failure modes in a busy cluster: a mutating admission webhook or policy engine that modifies CloudNativePG's Pods produces an endless rolling update, because every Pod the operator creates is changed by somebody else, so the record never matches what the operator would generate. The fix is to exclude those Pods from the mutation, not to make the operator less strict.

title: In-Place Instance Manager Upgrades
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster running the previous CloudNativePG release with the newer one staged and unapplied. Switch on in-place instance manager updates, upgrade the operator, and prove that every database Pod survived the version change untouched.
lectureNotes:
Part of the operator runs inside every database Pod

CloudNativePG is not only a controller in its own namespace. A binary from the operator image — the instance manager — runs as PID 1 in every postgres container, starting and stopping PostgreSQL, serving the probes, streaming the logs and answering the operator. PostgreSQL is its child process.

So the operator's version is two numbers, not one: the controller's, and the agent's inside each instance. The operator records the second on each Pod as the cnpg.io/operatorVersion annotation.

Why an operator upgrade restarts databases

When the controller moves to a new version, the agent has to follow. The ordinary way to change a binary inside a container is to replace the container, so by default upgrading the operator rolls every instance of every cluster it manages — replicas first, primary last, exactly as any other Pod spec change would. On an estate of clusters that turns an operator upgrade into database maintenance.

ENABLE_INSTANCE_MANAGER_INPLACE_UPDATES

Set that key to true in the operator's ConfigMap and the operator uploads the new binary to the running instance manager, which re-executes itself. The Pod is never deleted: the version annotation moves to the new release while creation timestamps stay where they were, restart counts stay at zero, and PostgreSQL's own uptime carries on across the upgrade.

Two traps sit around this setting, and both are silent. The key is spelled INPLACE, one word — ENABLE_INSTANCE_MANAGER_IN_PLACE_UPDATES is not recognised, and an unrecognised key in that ConfigMap is ignored with no error, no warning and no event. And the operator reads its ConfigMap only at startup, so the setting does nothing until the operator has been restarted. The reliable way to confirm both at once is to read the setting back out of the operator's own log: it prints its entire loaded configuration on startup, including enableInstanceManagerInplaceUpdates.

The trade is real rather than free — an in-place update replaces a running agent's binary underneath itself — which is why the conservative behaviour is the default and this is something you opt into.

title: Multi-Arch Images
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster on whatever processor architecture the host happens to be. Find out what you are running on, ask the registry directly what the pinned PostgreSQL tag actually contains, and follow the chain down to the file where an image states which architecture it was built for.
lectureNotes:
A tag names a list, not an image

On a modern registry a tag such as 18.4-system-trixie usually resolves to an index: a small document listing one image per platform, each with its own digest. When a node pulls the tag, the container runtime fetches the index, finds the entry whose platform matches itself, and pulls that one. Nothing in a CloudNativePG manifest mentions an architecture, and nothing has to — which is why the same manifests run unmodified on an Intel server and an Arm laptop.

Asking the registry yourself takes a token even for a public image, and an Accept header naming the index media type. Without that header a registry may convert its answer into something older and single-platform.

The entries that are not images

The index for the CloudNativePG PostgreSQL images lists four manifests: linux/amd64, linux/arm64, and two whose platform is unknown/unknown. Those two are not images at all — they are the build attestations, the signed provenance and software bill of materials published alongside. A runtime ignores them by matching on platform, which is exactly what you should do when reading the index by hand.

Where an image finally says what it is

The index entry is a claim about the image made by whoever assembled the index. The image makes the claim itself one level down: fetching the entry's digest returns a manifest, which names a small JSON blob called the config, and that blob carries architecture and os fields alongside the entrypoint, environment and layer history. Following index to manifest to config is the same walk the container runtime performed when it decided this image would run on this node.

Two practical consequences. Kubernetes exposes the architecture as the standard kubernetes.io/arch label on every node, so restricting a workload to one architecture is an ordinary node selector rather than a special mechanism. And pinning an image by digest is two different promises: an index digest keeps the multi-architecture property, while a single image's digest quietly ties the manifest to one architecture and will fail to schedule anywhere else.

title: Cluster Labels and Annotations
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a healthy database and everything the operator generated from it. Declare labels and annotations once on the Cluster and watch them reach a dozen objects, find out what removing one does not do, and then overwrite a label the operator was routing traffic on.
lectureNotes:
One field, every generated object

A label on a Cluster labels the Cluster. It does not label the Pods, the claims, the Services or the Secret the operator built from it — and those are what cost reporting, ownership queries and alert routing actually see. spec.inheritedMetadata is the per-cluster answer: labels and annotations declared once and copied by the operator onto everything it generates.

It applies within seconds and recreates nothing. Pod ages keep climbing, no connection is dropped, because this is a metadata update on live objects rather than a rolling update. Labels are selectable across kinds; annotations are not, and are for information such as an owner, a ticket or a runbook link.

Changing is not the mirror image of removing

Change a value and reconciliation rewrites it everywhere. Remove a key from the spec and absolutely nothing happens to the objects: the label stays on every Pod, claim, Service and Secret, indefinitely. Inheritance is additive — the operator applies what the spec asks for and keeps no record of what it once applied, so it cannot know that a label it is no longer asked for was its doing rather than yours.

There is a second trap on top of the first. A merge patch merges maps, so omitting a key does not remove it; removing one takes an explicit null. Together these mean an inherited label is a one-way door per object, and cleaning one up means labelling generated objects by hand — the very thing inheritance existed to avoid. Decide what belongs in the field before putting it there.

Inheritance has no guard rails

The operator applies inherited metadata after its own, so a key you inherit wins. Inherit cnpg.io/instanceRole as primary and all three instance Pods claim to be the primary; the read-write Service is only a selector, so it gains three endpoints, and writes start landing on read-only replicas with cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction. Nothing is wrong with the database — replication is fine and PostgreSQL is unaware — only with the sign on the door.

Removing the override repairs it within seconds, and the contrast with the previous section is the lesson: a label the operator does not care about is left behind forever, while one its own routing depends on is recomputed on every reconcile. Inherit keys in a namespace you own. cnpg.io/ belongs to the operator, and so does app.kubernetes.io/ on these objects.

title: Object Metadata
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a healthy database, and has you inventory everything the operator created through a single selector, read the labels that route traffic to the primary, and then try to move that traffic by editing a label yourself.
lectureNotes:
One label finds a whole cluster

You apply one object; the operator builds the rest. Every one of them — instance Pods, a PersistentVolumeClaim per instance, three Services, the application Secret, and the Jobs that create instances while they exist — carries cnpg.io/cluster naming the Cluster it came from. That single label is what makes a CloudNativePG cluster operable as a unit without knowing the naming convention for any of the kinds involved. Note that kubectl get all does not include claims or Secrets, so ask for them by name.

Alongside it, each object carries the Kubernetes-wide recommended labels under app.kubernetes.io/, which is what makes a CloudNativePG database legible to tooling that has never heard of the operator, plus a per-kind role label saying what the object is for: podRole=instance for a database Pod as opposed to a Job's Pod, pvcRole=PG_DATA for a data directory, userType=app for the application credentials. The annotations carry bookkeeping rather than identity — nodeSerial is the number in the instance's name and appears on both the Pod and its claim, which is how a rebuilt Pod finds the volume that belongs to it; operatorVersion records which operator built the object; pvcStatus notes that a claim has been initialised.

The labels are the routing table

A Service is a selector and a port. It cannot ask PostgreSQL anything and does not talk to the operator, so when pg-cluster-rw sends writes to the primary that is not cleverness — it selects cnpg.io/instanceRole=primary, and the operator's job is to make sure exactly one Pod carries that label. pg-cluster-ro selects instanceRole=replica and pg-cluster-r selects podRole=instance, every instance whatever its role. A failover, from the Service's point of view, is entirely a relabelling exercise. An older unprefixed role label is still written alongside the prefixed one for compatibility; new work should select on cnpg.io/instanceRole.

The operator owns its own keys

Relabel a replica as the primary with kubectl and the change survives well under a second — the operator watches these objects and recomputes the role from the cluster's real state on every event, so the label is corrected before the EndpointSlice controller has acted on it and no traffic ever moves. A label of your own on the same Pod is left untouched for the life of the Pod.

That is a narrow and useful promise: the operator does not enforce an identical copy of what it created, only the specific keys it depends on. Promotion is not something a label can do — the label is a consequence of the promotion — and your own metadata belongs under your own keys.

title: Data Corruption
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster with a real table on real disks. Damage one 8KB page inside it, watch the cluster go on reporting itself perfectly healthy, find the damage with the tool that looks for it, and recover the only way corruption can be recovered from.
lectureNotes:
Checksums catch bad bytes, but only when something reads them

A table is a file of 8KB pages, and with data checksums on every page carries a checksum of its own contents. A page whose checksum does not match is refused outright — ERROR: invalid page in block 3 of relation "base/16385/16390" — rather than being handed back as plausible-looking data.

The protection is real and its limit is important: it applies at read time. Nothing walks your files looking for damage, which is why corruption is so often discovered months later by a query nobody had run before. pg_stat_database.checksum_failures counts failed reads, not broken pages: it stays at zero until something touches the block, then increments. That makes it exactly the right thing to alert on and exactly the wrong thing to trust as a clean bill of health.

The one tool that goes looking is pg_checksums --check, which scans every block of every file and reports each mismatch with the checksum it calculated and the checksum the block claims, ending with a count of bad checksums. It refuses to run against a live server, so an instance has to be stopped for it — which fencing does without destroying the Pod.

Healthy is not the same as correct

The most uncomfortable part of this failure mode is how quiet it is. The container is Running, the readiness probe passes, the Cluster reports "Cluster in healthy state" with 3/3 ready, and the operator has no opinion at all. One query is an error and everything else in the system says the database is fine. Health checks answer "is this process serving?"; nothing in the stack answers "is this data intact?" unless you arrange for it.

Pages are not replicated; WAL records are

Damage on one instance's disk does not travel. Physical replication ships WAL records that describe changes, and each standby applies them to its own copy of the pages — so a block corrupted on one instance is fine everywhere else. That is what makes the recovery possible: you have two copies you have no reason to doubt.

The recovery, in order: move the writes off the damaged instance first, because while it is primary everything new is landing on a disk that has already lied once. Then discard its storage entirely and let the operator rebuild the instance from a good copy. There is no repairing a page; there is only replacing the copy that holds it. And be clear about the boundary — a replica saves you from damage that comes from below, from the storage. It does nothing about damage that comes from above, from a statement that deleted the wrong rows, because that is replicated faithfully within milliseconds. That one needs a backup you can restore to a moment before it happened.

title: Cloning a Cluster with pg_basebackup
description: This lab builds you a 3-node k3d cluster and a staged manifest that copies it. Stand up a full, writable, independent copy of a running database over the streaming replication protocol, then prove exactly how independent it is — starting with two rows that share an id and are not the same row.
lectureNotes:
One stanza, and one that is deliberately absent

bootstrap.pg_basebackup names an external cluster and takes a physical base backup of it over the streaming replication protocol, using the replication user and the source's certificates rather than an application password. What arrives is a byte-for-byte copy of the entire data directory: every database, every role, every setting — not one application's tables.

The field that decides what happens next is the one that is not there. A replica stanza would keep the copy in recovery, following the source indefinitely. Without it the copy starts up as its own primary the moment the backup finishes: pg_is_in_recovery() is false, there is no WAL receiver, and the source's pg_stat_replication never mentions it. The coupling lasted exactly as long as the copy took. You can watch the work happen — the operator runs it in a Job whose Pod is named <cluster>-1-pgbasebackup-… and the cluster reports "Setting up primary" while it runs.

Credentials are the one thing that does not come across unchanged

Every role arrives with its password, because the roles live inside the copied data directory. But the operator manages an application user for each Cluster it owns, so it resets that one to the password in the Secret it generated for the new cluster — and the source's application password is then refused with a plain authentication failure. Anything repointed at the copy needs the copy's Service and the copy's Secret.

A clone is not a backup

Write one row on each side afterwards and read the ids. Both sequences were copied at the same value and have been handed out independently ever since, so the same id now means two different rows, one per cluster, and nothing will ever reconcile them. That is the practical meaning of "independent copy", and it is why this shape belongs to testing and forensics rather than to disaster recovery.

One trap is worth naming. A clone taken this way is never promoted — it simply starts as a primary — so it does not begin a new timeline: source and copy both stay on timeline 1 while their WAL diverges. Never point one at the other's WAL archive and never let them share a backup destination, because nothing in the file names would tell them apart.

title: Importing a Database (Microservice)
description: This lab builds you a shared PostgreSQL server with several application databases on it. Take one of them off it and into a CloudNativePG cluster of its own with pg_dump and pg_restore, then find the two things the import did not bring: the roles, and everything written after it started.
lectureNotes:
A logical copy, taken at bootstrap

bootstrap.initdb.import is still an initdb bootstrap: a new empty database is created, and then the operator runs pg_dump against a source server and pipes it into pg_restore locally. Because it is logical — SQL, not files — it can take a single database out of a server that holds several, which a physical copy cannot.

The connection is an ordinary PostgreSQL connection over the network, described by an externalClusters entry, and it has to be made as a privileged user: pg_dump must read every object in the database, including those the application user does not own. On a CloudNativePG source that means switching on enableSuperuserAccess so a postgres password exists in a Secret.

What microservice means

type: microservice takes exactly one database and restores it into the new cluster's own application database. Two renamings follow from that and both surprise people: the database is no longer called what it was called — it is app — and the tables are no longer owned by the role that owned them, but by the new cluster's app user. The cluster that results is a normal CloudNativePG cluster with a generated application Secret, Services and certificates, indistinguishable from one created empty.

Roles are not part of it. The role that owned the tables on the old server does not exist on the new one, and neither does a read-only role that had been granted access to them. Anything that connected as one of those roles has nowhere to go.

The import is a moment, not a stream

pg_dump read the source once. A row written on the source a minute later exists only there, and nothing will fetch it: no replication slot, no WAL receiver, no subscription. That single fact defines the cutover — stop writing to the old database, import, verify, repoint the applications at the new Service with the new credentials, then start writing again. The outage is however long the dump and restore take, which is why the sensible move is to measure it on a copy first. If that window cannot be afforded, logical replication is the mechanism that closes it; this one does not.

title: Importing a Whole Server (Monolith)
description: This lab builds you a PostgreSQL server carrying several databases and the roles that own them. Lift the entire thing into a CloudNativePG cluster in one operation, verify what arrived down to the login passwords, and then look at what an imported cluster is missing that every other one has.
lectureNotes:
Moving a server rather than an application

type: monolith imports any number of databases and the roles they belong to, keeping the names and the ownership exactly as they were. Both lists accept "*" for everything, which is the lift-and-shift case; naming them individually is what you do when splitting a server rather than moving it. Grants come across with the objects, and roles keep their attributes — a role that cannot log in still cannot.

The dump is taken as a superuser over an ordinary network connection, described by an externalClusters entry, because pg_dumpall --roles-only and a dump of every database both require it.

Role passwords come with the roles

The roles dump carries password hashes, so a login role authenticates on the new cluster with the password it had on the old one. That is convenient during a migration and is worth planning for afterwards: once the copy exists, the same credentials open two different databases, and only one of them is the one people think they are talking to.

What an imported cluster does not have

A monolith import creates no application database, so the operator has no application user to manage: there is no -app Secret, only the ca, replication and server certificates the cluster needs to run. Every credential in the new cluster arrived in the dump and is yours to look after. Superuser access is off by default too, so postgres has no password and is reachable only through kubectl exec and peer authentication on the local socket — a better default than most old servers were running, and a different one.

And, as with any import, nothing replicates afterwards. The copy stopped when the import finished. What remains is a checklist rather than a mystery: repoint the applications at the new Services, decide which imported roles keep the passwords they arrived with, and create an application user yourself if you want the operator to manage one.

title: Storage Expansion
description: This lab builds you a cluster on a CSI driver whose volumes can actually be grown, alongside one whose cannot. Grow a running PostgreSQL instance's disk from 1Gi to 2Gi, watch the resize travel from the operator to the claim to the filesystem, and then walk into both of the walls the feature has.
lectureNotes:
Expansion is a property of the StorageClass

CloudNativePG cannot grow a volume on its own. It asks Kubernetes, Kubernetes asks the CSI driver, and whether that is possible at all is one field on the StorageClass: allowVolumeExpansion. Absent means false, and a request against such a class is refused by the API server before it reaches anybody else — only dynamically provisioned pvc can be resized and the storageclass that provisions the pvc must support resize. k3s's own local-path is one of those classes; a CSI driver's usually is not.

The two numbers that matter live in different places. spec.resources.requests.storage on the claim is what has been asked for and changes immediately; status.capacity.storage is what the volume actually is and follows a minute or so later. While they disagree, a resize is in flight.

What the resize actually does

Patching spec.storage.size on the Cluster writes the new size onto every claim, and the PVC's events then record the handoffs: ExternalExpanding as Kubernetes passes the request to the driver, Resizing as the driver grows the volume, FileSystemResizeRequired because a bigger volume is not a bigger filesystem, and FileSystemResizeSuccessful from the kubelet on the node once it is. When a resize gets stuck in production it is stuck at one of those four steps, and the events say which.

Nothing restarts. The Pod keeps its creation timestamp, the claim keeps its name, and — the check that distinguishes an expansion from a replacement — the volume behind the claim is the same volume it was before.

One direction only

Shrinking is refused by the operator's own validating webhook, naming both sizes: can't shrink existing storage from 2Gi to 1Gi. Kubernetes has no mechanism for making a volume smaller, and the refusal happens at admission so nothing is left half done.

Two decisions follow. Choosing a StorageClass is choosing whether your databases can ever be grown in place, and it cannot be revisited for volumes that already exist. And because expansion is one-way, the size you pick is a floor rather than a target: asking for too much costs money, asking for too little costs a migration.

title: A Dedicated WAL Volume
description: This lab builds you a 3-instance cluster whose data and write-ahead log share one disk. Give the WAL a volume of its own on the running cluster, see what the operator does to the data directory to arrange it, and then discover that this particular decision cannot be taken back.
lectureNotes:
Two very different streams of writes

PostgreSQL writes the write-ahead log sequentially and fsyncs it on every commit; it writes data files in scattered blocks whenever a checkpoint gets round to them. On one disk they compete, and the one that loses is the one every commit is waiting for. spec.walStorage gives the log a volume of its own.

Adding it to a running cluster works. The operator creates one <instance>-wal claim per instance and rolls the cluster to mount them — replicas first, primary last, restarted rather than switched over, about 45 seconds for three instances.

The mechanism is a symbolic link

Afterwards, pg_wal inside the data directory is no longer a directory: it is a link to /var/lib/postgresql/wal/pg_wal, which is where the second claim is mounted. PostgreSQL writes to the same path it always did and the filesystem sends those writes elsewhere — the same way separate WAL storage has always been arranged, and a good thing to recognise when reading somebody's data directory.

A detail that bites: the WAL claims are created on the *default* StorageClass unless walStorage.storageClass names one. If the data volumes are on fast storage chosen deliberately and the default class is something else, you have just moved the thing every commit waits for onto the slower disk.

It cannot be undone

Removing the field is refused by the operator's webhook: walStorage cannot be disabled once configured. Undoing it would mean moving live WAL back into the data directory while the database depends on it, and there is no safe automatic form of that.

So it is a decision to take when the cluster is created, or at least deliberately: size it for max_wal_size plus whatever wal_keep_size and any replication slots will retain — a WAL volume too small for those is a database that stops accepting writes — and name the StorageClass explicitly. The size can still be changed later, exactly like the data volume, provided the class allows expansion. The existence of the volume cannot.

title: Draining a Node
