description: This lab builds you a 3-instance cluster with one instance per node. Read the disruption budgets the operator maintains, drain a node for real and watch what gets stranded when a volume cannot follow its Pod, then use the field that tells CloudNativePG the drain was deliberate.
lectureNotes:
Two budgets, deliberately asymmetric

A drain cordons a node and then asks each Pod to leave, and an eviction can be refused. CloudNativePG maintains two PodDisruptionBudgets per cluster: one selecting cnpg.io/instanceRole=replica with minAvailable 1, which with two healthy replicas allows exactly one disruption, and one selecting the primary with minAvailable 1 over a single Pod, which allows none.

That second budget is why draining the primary's node behaves differently: the eviction is refused, the operator responds by moving the primary elsewhere, and the same eviction then succeeds on retry.

What a drain strands

On node-local storage the eviction is the easy part. A local-path volume is a directory on one machine, so an evicted instance can only be rescheduled onto the node it came from — which is the node you have just cordoned. The scheduler says so in one sentence: 0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) were unschedulable, 2 node(s) didn't match PersistentVolume's node affinity. The cluster sits degraded until the node comes back.

Watch for the other casualty. A Pod with no controller behind it is deleted by a drain and never returns, and the drain warns about it in a single line that is easy to miss: deleting Pods that declare no controller.

Telling the operator this was planned

spec.nodeMaintenanceWindow is the older lever. inProgress: true declares that maintenance is happening, and reusePVC: false answers the question that follows — should the operator wait for that volume, or write it off and rebuild the instance elsewhere from the copies still running? With reusePVC false the claim is deleted, a join Pod runs pg_basebackup from the primary, and the cluster is back to full redundancy in about a minute, at the cost of a full re-clone.

The API server answers that patch with a warning: Consider using .spec.enablePDB instead of the node maintenance window feature. The budgets are what make a drain safe by default now; the maintenance window remains for the case they cannot express, which is "this node is not coming back". And the reason any of it is delicate is the storage: with volumes that follow the Pod, the same drain is unremarkable.

title: Draining a Node with One Instance
description: This lab builds you a deliberately unreplicated cluster. Run into the disruption budget that refuses to let a drain take your only database instance down, then switch the budget off and find out precisely what it was protecting you from.
lectureNotes:
One instance leaves no room

A single-instance cluster gets exactly one PodDisruptionBudget — the one covering the primary — and its arithmetic has no slack: minAvailable 1 over one healthy Pod means zero allowed disruptions. ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS is computed, not configured, so there is no value of the budget that would behave differently.

What that does to a drain is worth seeing rather than reading about. The node is cordoned immediately — that part cannot be refused — and then the eviction is attempted, refused with Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget, retried every five seconds, and refused again until the command's timeout runs out. Without --timeout it waits forever. Meanwhile the database is entirely unaffected: still Running, still one endpoint behind the read-write Service, still taking writes.

Note that a failed drain still leaves the node cordoned. The cordon is not undone by the failure.

Turning the protection off does not remove the problem

spec.enablePDB: false deletes the budgets, and the same drain then completes in seconds. What follows is the outage the budget existed to prevent: the instance is evicted, its local-path volume belongs to the cordoned node, there is nowhere else it can run and no second copy to serve from. The Pod is Pending, the read-write Service has no endpoints at all, and a client gets connection refused. Uncordoning the node brings it back with the data intact — the outage cost availability, not data.

The order of preference is short. Give the cluster a replica first, and the problem disappears: with two instances the budgets have slack, the operator moves the primary and the drain succeeds. Failing that, schedule the outage, which is exactly the decision the budget is asking you to make. Disabling enablePDB is the third answer and its only honest use is a cluster that is genuinely disposable — the setting does not make the drain safe, it makes it quiet.

title: Declarative Hibernation
description: This lab builds you a 3-instance cluster and has you switch it off with a single annotation, keeping every volume. Find out what is still standing while it sleeps, edit its spec while it has no instances at all, and wake it up onto the disks it left behind.
lectureNotes:
One annotation, and it lives in your manifest

Hibernation has no field in the Cluster spec. It is the annotation cnpg.io/hibernation, and setting it to on is the whole interface — which is what makes it declarative: the annotation is part of the manifest, so whatever manages your manifests manages the sleeping too. Every instance Pod is removed within seconds, PostgreSQL having been shut down cleanly first, and every claim is left Bound. That difference — Pods gone, volumes kept — is the difference between hibernating a cluster and deleting one.

The status is the trap

kubectl get cluster reports "Cluster in healthy state" with a blank READY column. The operator is not lying: there is nothing unhealthy about a cluster that was asked to stop. But anything watching that column for trouble will not notice this at all. The honest signal is a condition — cnpg.io/hibernation, status True, reason Hibernated — and it is removed rather than set to False when the cluster wakes, so alerting has to treat absent as awake. ConsistentSystemID also goes False with reason NotFound, since no instance is left to report one.

What remains, and what that costs a client

The Services, the Secrets, the certificates and the claims all survive; only the Pods are gone. So the Service names still resolve and point at nothing, and a client gets connection refused rather than a DNS failure — a different problem to debug, and one that fools any check which treats a name resolving as a database being up.

The Cluster object stays an ordinary editable resource while it sleeps. A parameter changed with no instances running is simply in force when the instances start again, which makes hibernation a reasonable moment for changes you would rather not make to a running database.

Waking up takes about half a minute for three instances, and the proof that nothing was copied is an age mismatch: every Pod is younger than the claim it is using.

Hibernation suits a cluster that is genuinely idle and costs nothing but the storage you are paying for anyway. It is not a backup — the volumes are still the only copy — and it is not a way to protect a cluster you are worried about, because a hibernated cluster is one whose replication has stopped, whose backups have stopped, and which nobody is watching.

title: Hot and Cold Snapshot Backups
description: This lab builds you a cluster on a snapshot-capable CSI driver. Take one backup while the database runs and one with it stopped, find the difference recorded inside the snapshots themselves rather than in the documentation, and recover from the colder of the two.
lectureNotes:
One boolean, two very different operations

A volume snapshot is an instant copy of a disk, and a disk under a running database is being written to. spec.online on a Backup — or spec.backup.volumeSnapshot.online on the Cluster — decides how CloudNativePG deals with that.

Online, the default, takes the snapshot between pg_backup_start() and pg_backup_stop(). The database keeps serving; the second call returns a backup label recording where recovery must begin, and CloudNativePG stores it on the VolumeSnapshot as the cnpg.io/backupLabelFile annotation. Decoded, it is PostgreSQL's own backup_label: START WAL LOCATION, CHECKPOINT LOCATION, BACKUP METHOD: streamed, BACKUP FROM: primary.

Offline — cold — fences the target instance first. PostgreSQL shuts down cleanly, the snapshot is taken of a data directory nobody is writing to, and the fence is lifted. While it runs, the Cluster carries cnpg.io/fencedInstances naming the instance. There is no backup label because there is nothing in flight to replay.

The evidence is inside the snapshot

CloudNativePG also records the instance's control file on the snapshot, as cnpg.io/pgControldata. Read the one line that matters from each and the difference is unarguable: an online snapshot says Database cluster state: in production, a cold one says shut down. Two copies of the same database taken a minute apart, each carrying PostgreSQL's own account of what was true when it was made.

One field not to trust: in this operator release .status.online on the Backup reported true for both. Read .spec.online, which is what was asked for.

Choosing between them

Restoring is identical either way — a Cluster whose bootstrap.recovery.volumeSnapshots names the snapshot, and a claim whose dataSource is the VolumeSnapshot rather than an empty volume that was filled afterwards. A cold copy starts without recovery drama, its log reading "database system was shut down" and then "ready to accept connections".

Online is the right default: it costs nothing in availability and the label makes it perfectly restorable. Cold is for when you want a copy that needs no recovery at all, taken from a standby you can afford to lose for a minute. What you must not do is take a cold backup from a single-instance cluster without meaning to, because the instance that gets fenced is your database. Volume snapshots are attractive for large databases because the copy is instant regardless of size — but instant is a property of the storage, and consistency is still yours to arrange.

title: Point-in-Time Recovery from a Volume Snapshot
description: A snapshot restores you to the instant it was taken, which is rarely the instant you want. This lab builds a cluster on a snapshot-capable CSI driver that is also archiving its WAL to an object store. Take a hot snapshot and a cold one, write on both sides of a moment you record, and recover to that moment from each — proving that where you can recover to has nothing to do with how the snapshot was taken.
lectureNotes:
A snapshot is a floor, not a destination

Recovering from a volume snapshot on its own gives you the database exactly as it was when the snapshot was taken, and nothing after it. That is a useful thing to have and almost never the thing you want: the reason people restore is usually a statement run at 09:41, and the backup they hold was taken at midnight.

Point-in-time recovery is the pairing that fixes it. The snapshot supplies the data directory. The WAL archive supplies every change committed afterwards. A target time says where to stop replaying. The snapshot decides where recovery can start; the archive decides how far forward it can go.

The three parts of the manifest

bootstrap.recovery.volumeSnapshots names the VolumeSnapshot the data directory is restored from — the CSI driver creates a new volume from it, and the resulting claim records where it came from in spec.dataSource.

bootstrap.recovery.source names an entry under externalClusters, which in CloudNativePG 1.30 points at the object store through the Barman Cloud plugin. That is where the WAL is fetched from. Without it, the recovery has a starting point and nothing to replay.

recoveryTarget.targetTime is where to stop. Take the timestamp from the database's own clock — SELECT now() — not from a node's, because those are different clocks and recovery compares against the transaction log, not against your shell.

Hot and cold recover identically

An online snapshot carries a backup label recording where replay must begin. A cold one is a clean shutdown that needs no replay at all to open. That difference decides what happens when the copy is opened, and nothing else. Aim both at the same target time and both land on the same row: the same commits present, the same commits absent.

Which means the hot/cold choice is about what a backup costs you when you take it — a fenced instance or an uninterrupted one — and not about what it can do for you later. That is the archive's job.

Some practical notes

Recovery never overwrites the cluster you are recovering from: the result is a new Cluster with its own name, Services and credentials, and the original keeps serving throughout. Backups on one cluster serialize, so a second one applied immediately sits in pending until the first finishes. And it is worth switching WAL after your last write, so the segment holding it reaches the archive rather than sitting half-filled on the primary.

Volume snapshots are attractive for large databases because taking one is instant however big the volume is, and restoring is a storage operation rather than a copy. Pairing them with an archive is what turns "a copy of last night" into "the database as it was at 09:41" — and that second thing is what people mean when they ask whether you have backups.

title: Snapshot Backups with the cnpg Plugin
description: Taking a backup right now, because somebody is about to do something frightening, is not a moment for writing YAML. This lab builds a cluster on a snapshot-capable CSI driver and hands you the kubectl cnpg plugin. Take one backup with no flags, one with the flag that stops the database first, and then read what the plugin actually created.
lectureNotes:
A command that builds an object

kubectl cnpg backup does not take a backup. It builds an ordinary Backup resource out of its flags, applies it, and prints the name. The operator then does exactly what it would have done for a manifest you wrote by hand. That is the whole design, and it is why the plugin is safe to reach for under pressure: there is no second mechanism to reason about afterwards.

The flags map one to one onto the resource. -m/--method is spec.method. --online is spec.online. --backup-name is the object's name. -t/--backup-target overrides which instance is used. --immediate-checkpoint and --wait-for-archive set the two fields of spec.onlineConfiguration.

Defaults come from the cluster, and it shows

Run it with no flags beyond the method and the plugin leaves spec.online unset. The field reads <none> in a custom-columns listing, and the Cluster's own spec.backup.volumeSnapshot.online decides what happens. Pass --online=false and the field reads false.

That distinction is worth reading carefully in somebody else's cluster: an empty field means "whatever the cluster does", a set one means "somebody asked for this deliberately". They can produce the same backup today and different ones tomorrow.

The name is a small thing that matters

With no --backup-name the plugin composes one from the cluster's name and a timestamp — pg-cluster-20260817011046. That is unambiguous and completely unmemorable. A backup you may need to find in a hurry, or hand to somebody else, deserves a name you chose.

What the snapshot itself records

An offline backup is implemented by fencing the target instance: the operator stops PostgreSQL inside the Pod without deleting it, takes the snapshot, and lifts the fence. While it runs, cnpg.io/fencedInstances on the Cluster names the instance. On a replicated cluster the default target is a standby, so the cost is a replica for half a minute; on a single-instance cluster the cost is the database.

Afterwards the evidence lives in the snapshot's annotations, not in your memory. cnpg.io/pgControldata records the control file — Database cluster state: in production for an online copy, shut down for a cold one — and only online snapshots carry cnpg.io/backupLabelFile, because there was no running server to bracket with pg_backup_start and pg_backup_stop.

What the cluster keeps track of

status.lastSuccessfulBackup, status.firstRecoverabilityPoint and status.lastSuccessfulBackupByMethod are maintained by the operator, and the last of those is the one that stops you drawing the wrong conclusion: a recoverability point means nothing until you know which method produced it. kubectl cnpg status shows the same material under Continuous Backup status, including whether WAL archiving is working and the last segment archived.

title: Scheduled Snapshot Backups, and Who Deletes Them
description: A backup you have to remember to take is not a backup. This lab builds a cluster on a snapshot-capable CSI driver and two staged ScheduledBackups. Run one online and one that fences the database on every firing, watch them accumulate — and then confront the part nobody mentions until the storage bill arrives: nothing prunes old volume snapshots, and whether deleting a backup takes its snapshot with it is a field you have to set.
lectureNotes:
A Backup with a clock attached

A ScheduledBackup carries the same fields as a one-off Backup — the cluster, the method, whether it runs online — plus a schedule and a couple of fields about when to start. When it fires it creates an ordinary Backup named after the schedule with a timestamp appended, and from there nothing is different.

The schedule field has six fields, not five. CloudNativePG counts seconds first, so "0 * * * * *" is second zero of every minute. A five-field expression pasted in from a crontab will not mean what it means there, and the feedback loop on that mistake is long.

immediate: true runs it once at creation. That is convenient in a lab and a good habit anywhere: a schedule that has never fired is a schedule nobody has tested.

Three timestamps worth monitoring

status carries lastCheckTime (when the operator last looked), lastScheduleTime (when it last fired) and nextScheduleTime (when it will fire next). A schedule whose lastScheduleTime has stopped moving is a backup that has stopped happening, and nothing else in the cluster will raise its voice about it. Watch that field rather than the cluster's phase.

suspend: true stops the clock without deleting the schedule or anything it has made — the right tool for an incident, a migration, or any window where fencing the database would be unwelcome.

online: false, every time, forever

A schedule inherits the same fencing behaviour as a one-off offline backup: the instance is stopped, the snapshot is taken of a quiet data directory, the fence is lifted. Doing that once deliberately is reasonable. Doing it on a schedule means a small outage on the target instance on every run, without anybody being asked again. On a single-instance cluster, that instance is the database.

Schedules also collide. Two of them firing at second zero of the same minute contend for the same cluster, and an online run that lands while a cold one has the instance fenced fails with "while ensuring target pod is healthy: no status found for target pod". Stagger the seconds rather than pointing every schedule at zero.

Nothing prunes volume snapshots

This is the finding that matters most. Retention policies you may have seen belong to Barman and apply to what Barman writes to an object store. A VolumeSnapshot is a Kubernetes object created by the CSI driver, and CloudNativePG does not delete them. A schedule left running turns quietly into an unbounded number of full-size copies of your volume.

What you can control is whether deleting a Backup takes its snapshot with it. spec.backup.volumeSnapshot.snapshotOwnerReference defaults to none, and with that default the snapshot carries no ownerReferences at all: delete the Backup and the snapshot stays behind, now with nothing pointing at it. Set the field to backup and the next snapshot carries ownerReferences: Backup/<name> and disappears with its Backup through ordinary Kubernetes garbage collection. cluster is the third option, tying the snapshot's life to the Cluster instead.

So the operational shape is: choose online or offline deliberately, because the schedule will not ask again; monitor lastScheduleTime; set snapshotOwnerReference if you want deletions to cascade; and own the retention yourself, because nothing here will do it for you.

title: Managed Roles: Declaring Who Can Log In
description: Every database grows a collection of roles, and the usual way they arrive — somebody runs CREATE ROLE once and writes the password in a ticket — is exactly why nobody can say what the current set is. This lab has you declare a role in the Cluster instead, with its password in a Secret, and then find the two edges that matter more than the happy path: what the operator does when somebody changes a role behind its back, and what it does when you ask it to drop a role that still owns something.
lectureNotes:
Roles as part of the cluster's definition

spec.managed.roles is a list of the roles a cluster should have. Each entry is a name, an ensure of present or absent, the attributes the role should carry — login, createdb, superuser, connectionLimit, inRoles, comment — and, optionally, a passwordSecret naming a Kubernetes Secret that holds the password.

That last part is the point. The password lives in a Secret, so it can be rotated, sealed, sourced from a vault or audited like any other Kubernetes object, and it never appears in a manifest or in anybody's shell history. The Secret needs both a username and a password key, and the operator checks that username matches the role it is managing — a small guard against pointing a role at the wrong Secret.

Reading the status

status.managedRolesStatus sorts every role in the database. byStatus.reserved holds the ones the operator uses itself and will not let you manage: postgres, streaming_replica and the metrics exporter. byStatus.not-managed holds roles that exist but that nothing has asked for, which is where app starts. Roles you declare move into byStatus.reconciled. passwordStatus records the Secret's resourceVersion and the transaction id in which the password was applied, which is how the operator knows whether the Secret has changed since.

Applied on change, not enforced continuously

This is the finding that shapes how much you can lean on the mechanism. Take a managed role's LOGIN away in SQL — the way somebody would during an incident — and the operator does not put it back. Not after a minute, not after five. The status goes on reporting the role as reconciled the whole time, because the operator compares against what it last applied rather than against what the database currently says.

Any later change to the spec makes it re-apply the whole entry, and the drift disappears at that moment. Note that it re-applies the entry rather than the field you touched: spec.managed.roles is a list and a merge patch replaces it wholesale, so an entry sent without its login or its passwordSecret loses them.

The practical reading: managed roles are excellent for describing the roles a cluster should have and for keeping their passwords in Kubernetes. They are not an audit control, and they will not tell you somebody has been editing roles by hand.

ensure: absent is a request, not a guarantee

Whether a role can be dropped is PostgreSQL's decision. A role that owns objects cannot be, and declaring harder does not help. The operator handles the refusal well: it does not fail the cluster, does not retry forever in the background and does not hide the problem. The role moves to byStatus.pending-reconciliation and PostgreSQL's own answer appears in cannotReconcile — could not perform DELETE on role analyst: 2 objects in database app, where the two objects are a table and the sequence behind its serial column.

Two habits follow. Reassign or drop what a role owns before asking for it to be absent; REASSIGN OWNED BY and DROP OWNED BY are what a real retirement looks like. And alert on status.managedRolesStatus.cannotReconcile rather than on the cluster's phase, because this is a class of failure that leaves the cluster perfectly healthy and the request quietly unfulfilled.

title: Password Maintenance with Kubernetes Secrets
description: A password in a Secret is only useful if changing the Secret changes the password. This lab hands you a managed role whose password lives in one, has you rotate it and watch the database go on accepting the old password, and then find the single line that was missing. After that: what the operator does when somebody changes the password in SQL, and the two declarative ways to take a password away.
lectureNotes:
The label is the mechanism

A managed role's password lives in a Kubernetes Secret, named by passwordSecret. Editing that Secret is the obvious way to rotate the password, and on a Secret you created by hand it does nothing at all — the old password goes on working indefinitely.

CloudNativePG only watches Secrets that carry the label cnpg.io/reload: "true". Everything else is read once, when the spec naming it changes, and then never looked at again. The operator's own generated Secrets — pg-cluster-app and the rest — carry the label, which is exactly why the mechanism is invisible until you make a Secret yourself. Add it and the rotation you asked for a minute ago is applied within seconds.

Two resourceVersions, and the gap between them

status.managedRolesStatus.passwordStatus records, per role, the resourceVersion of the Secret the operator last applied and the transaction id it applied it in. Compare that number with the Secret's current metadata.resourceVersion and you have a one-line diagnosis of whether a rotation has landed.

Nothing else reports it. The cluster stays healthy and byStatus keeps the role under reconciled whether the two agree or not, because the operator is not claiming the database matches the Secret — it is claiming it applied what it was given, which is true.

Drift, and the fix for it

Change a managed role's password in SQL and the operator does not put it back. The comparison it makes is Secret-version against applied-version, so a change made in the database is not something it is looking at.

The fix follows from that: you do not need to change the password to force a re-apply, you need to change the Secret. Any change moves its resourceVersion — an annotation is enough — and the operator overwrites the database with what the Secret says on its next poll. "Touch the Secret" is the operational answer to any password drift you find.

Ending a password rather than changing it

validUntil is written straight through to PostgreSQL's VALID UNTIL. Set one in the past and the client gets FATAL: password authentication failed for user "analyst" — the same sentence a wrong password produces. PostgreSQL does not tell the client the password expired, and the operator still reports the role as reconciled, so an expiry nobody remembers looks exactly like a typo. Moving the date forward is the whole of a renewal.

disablePassword: true sets the password to NULL. It cannot be combined with a passwordSecret: asking for both is refused at admission with "This role both sets and disables a password". Afterwards rolpassword is NULL, no password gets in, and the role may still log in — it simply has nothing to log in with, which is what you want for a role that authenticates by certificate or by peer instead.

One detail worth carrying: the operator re-applies the entire role entry, not the field you edited. Dropping validUntil from the entry sent rolvaliduntil back to infinity, and once no Secret is named, passwordStatus keeps only a transaction id, with no resourceVersion to compare.

title: Declarative Tablespaces
description: A tablespace is a directory PostgreSQL may put relations in; in Kubernetes a directory is a volume. This lab has you declare two tablespaces on a running cluster, watch the operator create one claim per instance for each of them, follow a table down to the symlink that implements it, and then find the one thing the mechanism will not let you do.
lectureNotes:
One declaration, one volume per instance

spec.tablespaces is a list of names and storage blocks. What the operator does with an entry is more than a CREATE TABLESPACE: every instance needs its own copy of the directory, because a standby replays the primary's writes into files of its own. So one tablespace on a three-instance cluster is three PersistentVolumeClaims, named <instance>-tbs-<tablespace> and labelled cnpg.io/pvcRole: PG_TABLESPACE with cnpg.io/tablespaceName.

Attaching a volume means replacing the Pods, so declaring a tablespace rolls the cluster — about a minute for three instances, with the phase moving through "Waiting for the instances to become active" and "Primary instance is being restarted without a switchover". Meanwhile each tablespace reports its own progress in status.tablespacesStatus, from pending to reconciled.

Where it actually lives

Inside the container the volume is mounted at /var/lib/postgresql/tablespaces/<name>, and pg_tablespace_location reads /var/lib/postgresql/tablespaces/<name>/data. The implementation is visible in the data directory: pg_tblspc holds one symlink per tablespace, named after its OID, pointing at that mount. Everything written to the tablespace goes through that link, onto that claim, and not onto the instance's main data volume.

Using one is ordinary SQL — CREATE TABLE ... TABLESPACE reporting — and nothing about Kubernetes appears in the statement. pg_tables.tablespace records the choice, and every replica shows the same table in the same tablespace, in its own physical copy.

What the webhook fills in

Read the spec back after applying it and there are fields nobody wrote: owner defaults to the application user, temporary to false, and storage.resizeInUseVolumes to true. Defaulting happens at admission, so the document you sent and the one the cluster holds are not the same — which matters because the list is replaced wholesale by a merge patch.

The refusal

A tablespace cannot be undeclared. Sending the list without one is rejected at admission: "no tablespace can be deleted once created". That is deliberate — a tablespace may hold relations, and the operator has no way to know what dropping it would cost you — and it makes adding one a decision about the shape of every instance for as long as the cluster exists. The storage stays attached even if you drop everything in it.

Two practical consequences. Every later change to the list has to resend every tablespace you already have. And the count of volumes you are paying for is tablespaces × instances, not tablespaces.

title: Temporary Tablespaces
description: A query that exceeds work_mem writes the difference to disk, and by default that disk is the one holding your database. This lab has you declare a temporary tablespace, watch a sort spill 99 megabytes into it while the data directory stays empty, and then send a big read to a standby to find out whose storage that one uses.
lectureNotes:
One field on a tablespace entry

Every entry under spec.tablespaces carries a temporary boolean. Set it and the tablespace is created exactly like any other — a claim per instance, mounted, then CREATE TABLESPACE — and its name is also written into PostgreSQL's temp_tablespaces setting, the list the server consults when it needs somewhere to put a temporary object or a spilled sort.

Because attaching a volume replaces the Pods, this rolls the cluster; the tablespace goes pending → reconciled in about a minute. Afterwards every instance reports temp_tablespaces = scratch, not just the primary.

Two kinds of temporary

Temporary objects are relations, so they get a tablespace and pg_class.reltablespace records it: a CREATE TEMP TABLE lands in scratch. Ask about it in the same psql invocation that created it, because a temporary table dies with its session.

Temporary files are what a query writes when it exceeds work_mem — sort runs, hash batches, materialised results. Nothing in the catalogue records them, so watch the directory during the query and the counters afterwards. With work_mem at 64kB, a 300,000-row sort grew the scratch volume to 99M while it ran and left it at 20K when the session ended, taking pg_stat_database's temp_files from 1 to 3 and temp_bytes from 2734 kB to 107 MB.

The evidence is emptiness, not absence

PostgreSQL creates base/pgsql_tmp inside the data directory at startup whether or not a temporary tablespace exists. With one set, that directory stays at 4.0K with zero entries while the files pile up in a pgsql_tmp of the tablespace's own. So the thing to check is that it stayed empty — not that it is missing.

Standbys spill too, into their own

A read-only query sorts exactly like a write does, and a standby cannot borrow the primary's disk. That is why the tablespace is created on every instance. Send a large sort through the -ro Service and the counters tell you which standby served it: one reported 2 files and 22 MB, the other nothing at all, while pg_is_in_recovery() was true on both.

Two consequences. pg_stat_database is per-instance and is not replicated, so monitoring has to scrape every instance to see spilling at all. And the temporary storage you provision has to be sized for the largest query any single instance might serve — while being the one volume in the cluster whose contents are worth nothing, since they are deleted when the query that owned them ends.

title: Declarative Databases
description: A CloudNativePG cluster arrives with exactly one application database, and the usual way a second appears is somebody running CREATE DATABASE and telling nobody. The Database resource makes it an object instead. This lab has you declare one, find out what happens when two objects claim the same database, and then delete the object to see what that does — and does not — do to the data.
lectureNotes:
A database as an object

Database is a namespaced resource with a small spec: which Cluster hosts it, what the database is called in PostgreSQL, and who owns it. The object's name and the database's name are separate fields, which is what lets two clusters in one namespace both have a reporting.

Apply it and the operator issues the CREATE DATABASE, then reports in the object's own status rather than in a log: applied, an observedGeneration, and a message when something went wrong. It took about twelve seconds in a real run, and the result is an ordinary database reachable through the ordinary Services — there is nothing special about it afterwards.

What arrives without you

Read the stored object and three things are there that the manifest never said: ensure: present, databaseReclaimPolicy: retain, and the finalizer cnpg.io/deleteDatabase. The finalizer is the interesting one: it exists so that deleting the object is not merely a Kubernetes deletion — the operator gets to decide what happens to the PostgreSQL database first, and the reclaim policy is how you tell it what you want.

One object owns one database

Apply a second object naming the same PostgreSQL database and the apply succeeds — the object is valid, and this is not something admission can settle. The operator resolves it afterwards and refuses the newcomer in that object's own status: applied: false, "reporting" is already managed by object "reporting-db". The first object is untouched and the database is not disturbed, so the conflict is contained inside the object that caused it.

Retain, and adoption

The default reclaim policy is retain, and it governs exactly one moment: what happens when the object is deleted. Under retain the answer is nothing — the finalizer is removed, the object goes, and the database and its rows stay. That default is chosen for the obvious reason: objects get deleted by mistaken commands, by namespace cleanups and by reconcilers pruning what they no longer see in Git, and none of those should drop a database.

What makes retain useful rather than merely safe is adoption. Re-apply the same manifest and the operator does not fail because the database exists and does not recreate it — it takes it back under management, applied: true, with the data intact. That is the recovery path after a namespace was rebuilt or a manifest moved between repositories.

Two cautions. Adoption is by name, so an object pointed at an existing database it was never meant to manage will take it over, and the only protection is that a second claim on the same database is refused. And a database left behind by a deleted object keeps its storage and its cost, with nothing in Kubernetes left to remind you it is there.

title: Database Reclaim Policies
description: When a Database object is deleted, should the data go with it? CloudNativePG makes that an explicit field with two values. This lab runs both policies side by side on one cluster, deletes both objects — one of them while a client is still connected — and separates the three different fields that can each end with a database gone.
lectureNotes:
Two values, one moment

databaseReclaimPolicy is retain or delete, and it governs exactly one moment: what happens to the PostgreSQL database when the Kubernetes object is deleted. retain, the default, leaves it alone. delete drops it. While the object exists the field does nothing at all, which is why it is easy to set carelessly and easy to forget.

A deletion that cannot finish

PostgreSQL will not drop a database anybody is connected to, so deleting a delete-policy object while a session is open blocks. The object stays listed with a deletionTimestamp set and its cnpg.io/deleteDatabase finalizer still attached, the database is still there, and a plain kubectl delete simply does not return.

What is missing from that picture is any explanation. In a real run there was no event on the object, no message in its status — which still read applied: true — and no line in the operator's log naming the database. The only signals are the command not returning and the object still being listed. The moment the session ended, the object went and the database was dropped.

The operational reading: with delete, removing the object is a destructive database operation wearing Kubernetes clothes, and it can hang indefinitely on something as ordinary as an idle connection from an application nobody has scaled down. It suits genuinely disposable databases — preview environments, per-branch databases, test fixtures — and nothing you would miss.

ensure is a different field

ensure: absent also ends with the database gone, and it is not the same thing. It is a statement about the database while the object exists: the operator drops it and goes on reconciling the object, which stays in the namespace still reporting applied: true. Set it on an object whose reclaim policy is retain and the database goes anyway — the policy was never consulted, because the object was never deleted.

Three separate decisions live in this resource, and confusing them is how data goes missing. Whether the database exists right now is ensure. What happens to it if the object is deleted is databaseReclaimPolicy. Whether the operator is managing it at all is whether an object exists — which is why a database left behind by retain is invisible to Kubernetes until somebody declares it again.

One is reversible in the ordinary way: change ensure back and the operator creates the database again, empty. The other only fires when there is no longer an object to change your mind with.

title: Backing Up a Cluster with Tablespaces
description: A base backup of a cluster with tablespaces contains the tablespaces, and restoring it needs somewhere to put them — which in Kubernetes means a volume somebody asked for. This lab has you take the backup, try the recovery that forgets, read the failure it produces, and then do it properly.
lectureNotes:
Taking it is the easy half

A Backup with method: plugin hands the work to the Barman Cloud plugin, which copies the data directory and the tablespaces into the bucket. On a small database it finishes in seconds, and by default it runs against a standby — the backup label records BACKUP FROM: standby and the status names the Pod it used, so the primary is never touched.

The status also records beginWal and beginLSN. That first field matters more than it looks.

A completed backup is not always a restorable one

Recovery needs the whole WAL segment the backup begins in, and a base backup begins somewhere inside a segment that is still being written. On a busy database the segment fills and ships by itself. On an idle one it stays open indefinitely, and the restore fails with checking the presence of first needed WAL in the archive: object storage or file not found … WAL not found — weeks later, when somebody actually needs it.

One statement fixes it: SELECT pg_switch_wal() on the primary, after the backup. Compare pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn()) with the backup's beginWal and you can see the difference between a backup you have and a backup you can use.

The recovery manifest has to declare the tablespaces

Recovery creates a new Cluster from the manifest you give it, and that manifest is the only thing that decides which volumes the new cluster gets. Declare no tablespaces and no tablespace volumes are created — while the backup still contains them.

What that produces is worth recognising. barman-cloud-restore unpacks the data directory, reaches the tablespace and tries to write into /var/lib/postgresql/tablespaces, which exists inside the image but has no volume mounted over it on a container whose root filesystem is read-only. The Job Pod fails with Barman cloud restore exception: [Errno 30] Read-only file system: '/var/lib/postgresql/tablespaces', is replaced, and fails again. Meanwhile the Cluster sits at Setting up primary indefinitely and its own status says nothing about why. The error lives only in the logs of Pods named <cluster>-1-full-recovery-…, which are being deleted and recreated while you look for them.

Adding a tablespaces block naming the same tablespace is the whole fix: the operator creates the claim before the restore job runs, mounts it where the backup expects it, and the cluster comes up healthy in about forty seconds with the table still in its tablespace and the pg_tblspc symlink rebuilt.

Two things that do not have to match

The recovery cluster's instance count is yours to choose — a single instance can recover a three-instance cluster's backup, and it needs one volume per tablespace because it has one instance. The tablespace *names*, on the other hand, must match what is inside the backup, and nothing checks that for you until the restore job opens it.

title: Snapshot Backups of a Cluster with Tablespaces
description: A volume snapshot copies one volume, and a cluster with a tablespace has more than one — so its snapshot backup is a set of snapshots, and recovery is a mapping you have to write by hand. This lab has you take the backup, try a recovery that maps only half of it, find where the operator says so, and then map every volume back.
lectureNotes:
One snapshot per volume

A Backup with method: volumeSnapshot copies the instance's volumes, and a cluster with a tablespace has two of them. So the backup produces two VolumeSnapshots: the data volume's takes the Backup's name, and each tablespace's is that name with -tbs-<tablespace> appended. The tablespace's snapshot also carries the label cnpg.io/tablespaceName, which is the reliable way to tell them apart.

Nothing joins the set together but that shared name and those labels. There is no single object a recovery can point at and have the rest worked out.

Recovery is a mapping, and it is unchecked

bootstrap.recovery.volumeSnapshots has a storage field for the data directory and a tablespaceStorage map from tablespace name to snapshot. Leave the map out and the manifest is still valid — the cluster declares a tablespace, and nothing at admission time compares that with the recovery block.

What follows is silence rather than an error: one data claim Pending on WaitForFirstConsumer, no tablespace claim, no Pod, an empty cluster phase, and events about creating a ServiceAccount. kubectl describe says nothing; the conditions even claim the cluster has been bootstrapped. The reason exists in exactly one place, the operator's log: cannot create primary instance PVCs: missing StorageSource for tablespace reporting PVC.

That generalises. When a CloudNativePG cluster does nothing at all — no Pod, no events, no phase — the operator log is where the answer is, because a controller that cannot proceed has nowhere else to write.

With every volume mapped, recovery is ordinary: the operator creates both claims from their snapshots, the instance starts on a data directory whose pg_tblspc symlink already points at a restored volume, and it is healthy in about forty seconds. Each claim's spec.dataSource records which snapshot built it, which is the artefact that proves the mapping was what you meant.

A naming trap worth knowing

Do not put -tbs- in the name of a cluster that has tablespaces. A tablespace's claim is named <instance>-tbs-<tablespace>, and the operator parses that shape to decide which claims are tablespaces — so a cluster called pg-tbs-restored had its own data claim read as a tablespace's.

The symptom is unpleasant precisely because everything else looks right: the data restores correctly, both claims bind, the rows are all there, and the cluster rolls its instance every twenty seconds forever, logging original and target PodSpec differ in volumes: element tbs-pgdata has been removed. Renaming the cluster, with nothing else changed, brought it up healthy in 36 seconds and it stayed that way.

title: Declarative Major Version Upgrade
description: A minor upgrade is a restart on a new binary; a major upgrade rewrites the catalogue. This lab hands you a PostgreSQL 17 cluster and one field to change, has you watch the pg_upgrade job the operator runs and the replica rebuild that follows, and then find the three things the upgrade leaves you to deal with — including the one that cannot be undone.
lectureNotes:
One field, a different operation

The interface for a major upgrade is `spec.imageName`, the same field a minor upgrade uses. What makes it a different operation is that the operator remembers which image last ran on the data directory, in status.pgDataImageInfo — image and majorVersion — and compares. When the major differs it does not roll the cluster: it stops the database and runs pg_upgrade against the existing data directory in place, with the phase reading "Upgrading Postgres major version".

How pg_upgrade gets both installations

pg_upgrade needs the old binaries as well as the new ones, and an operand image carries exactly one PostgreSQL. The Job the operator creates, <primary>-major-upgrade, solves that with three containers: an init container from the operator image, an init container called prepare running the **old** image, and a main container called major-upgrade running the **new** one.

The prepare container's log spells out its job — "Copying the PostgreSQL installation to the destination /controller/old" — followed by /usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin, /usr/lib/postgresql/17/lib, /usr/share/postgresql/17 and a bindir.txt recording where they landed. That is pg_upgrade's --old-bindir. The consequence: the old image must still be pullable when you upgrade, so a tag deleted from your registry is a tag you cannot upgrade away from.

Asymmetric by design: one volume kept, the rest rebuilt

The primary is upgraded in place and keeps its claim and its PersistentVolume. The replicas cannot be — their data directories were written by the old major — so the operator deletes them and clones them again with the ordinary <instance>-join Jobs, the same ones that build a brand-new replica, while the phase reads "Creating a new replica".

The volumes are the evidence: on a three-instance cluster afterwards, one claim is as old as the cluster and two are minutes old. On a real database that rebuild, not pg_upgrade, is what takes the time — every replica is a fresh pg_basebackup of the whole database.

There is no way back

Editing the image to the old major is refused at admission: spec.imageName: Invalid value: "17": can't downgrade from major 18 to 17. Nothing is written, so nothing is broken — but nothing is reversible either, and no copy of the old cluster is kept: the volume holds one pgdata directory and that is now the new major. The route back to the old version is a backup taken before the upgrade, restored into a cluster that still names the old image.

Two things the upgrade does not bring

Optimizer statistics do not survive pg_upgrade. Afterwards reltuples reads -1 — PostgreSQL's marker for "never analysed" — and pg_stats holds nothing for any column. The database is up and the planner is guessing, so ANALYZE (in practice vacuumdb --analyze-in-stages) is the last step of the upgrade rather than an optional tidy-up.

And an upgraded cluster keeps the decisions initdb made under the *old* version, because no initdb ever ran. Data checksums show it plainly: PostgreSQL 18's initdb enables them and 17's did not, so an upgraded cluster reports data_checksums off while one freshly bootstrapped from the very same image reports on. Nothing is wrong — but "we are on 18 now" does not mean "we have what 18 would have given us", and checksums in particular can only be enabled later with the database shut down.
